parties:
Karimon Nessa being dead her heir Chand Ali Pramanik and others ------ Petitioners
vs.
Sorab Ali and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
2. The relevant facts necessary for disposal of this Rule are that Karimon Nessa, deceased mother of the present plaintiff petitioners, instituted the above noted original suit for having a declaration of title in the suit land measuring 3.37 acres as described in the schedule "G" to the plaint. According to her case, 'ka' schedule land measuring an area of 5.00 acres including the suit land as recorded under CS Khatian No. 56 previously belonged to 3 sisters namely; Golejan Bibi and Sukjan Bibi in equal shares. Rupejan Bibi died leaving her heirs in 2 sisters. Thereafter, Golejan Bibi died leaving her husband Saimuddin and sister Sukjan Bibi, Subsequently, Sukjan Bibi died leaving the plaintiff Karimon Nessa as daughter, who also got the share of Saimuddin by purchase. That the plaintiff and Golejan Bibi previously transferred 0.87 acres of land to Ayet Ali who has also possession therein. SA Khatian in respect of the said transferred land along with the some other lands were prepared accordingly in the name of the plaintiff and Ayet Ali, which is shown in schedule 'Kha' to the plaint. That when the plaintiff was the actual owner and possessor of the remaining 'Ga' schedule land (suit land) it was once sold in auction on 21-11-1953 in Rent Execution Case No. 770 of 1953 and ex-landlord was shown to have purchased the land paper, but possession was never delivered to him after the said auction sale. Thereafter, the plaintiff filed the Miscellaneous Case No. 26 of 1959, in the 3rd Court of Munsif, Pabna for setting aside the auction sale under section 174(3) of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Accordingly, the disputed auction sale was set aside in the proceeding by the learned Munsif vide an order dated 23-5-1959. Therefore, the suit land remained under the ownership of the plaintiff as it was before. But subsequently, during SA operation, the suit land was wrongly recorded as khas land of the Government (defendant No. 1) on the basis of said wrong SA Khatian. Two lease cases were collusively started in the years 1970-71 and lease order was issued in favour of the defendant No. 2 Sobhan Ali Sheikh. On being aware of the aforesaid, settlement to the defendant No. 2 on 10-4-1975, the plaintiff filed the present suit for having a declaration of her title in the suit property. The defendant No. 1, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, did not contest the suit. The defendant No. 2 Md Sorab Ali Sheikh contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the 'Ka' Schedule land originally belonged to Kachir Mondal who died leaving 3 daughters namely, Golejan Bibi, Rupjan Bibi and Sukjan Bibi, one wife Moyful and 3 cousins (paternal) namely; Biru, Hiru and Miru. Rapjan Bibi died leaving her husband Gumani Mridha, mother Moyful and 2 sisters Golejan and Sukjan. Thereafter Sukjan Bibi died leaving her husband Pabna, mother Moyful, sister Golejan Bibi and daughter (plaintiff). Then Moyful died leaving her daughter Golejan Bibi, second husband Bina Mondal and daughter Elajan. Thereafter, Golejan Bibi died leaving her husband Saimuddin and Cousin Subid Mondal Miru Mondal was survived by his only son Subid Mondal. Hiru Mondal died unmarried leaving his brother Biru Mondal, Elajan, daughter of Biru Mondal, died leaving her father and 2 daughters in Sakina and Bashabi Bewa. Biru Mondal left his second wife Tolajan and nephew Mondal as heirs. Thereafter Subid Mondal, Tolajan Bibi and Pabna (husband of Sukja) sold 2.97 acres of land by 2 registered Kabalas dated 2-4-1968 and 12-4-1968. Subsequently, when the defendant No. 2 found that the suit land was sold in auction sale and the Government acquired ownership, he took lease from the Government vide Settlement Case No. 9 of 1970-71 and 14 of 1970-71 and continued possession in the suit property. The plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 410 of 1968 against the Government for correction of record, which was dismissed. So, the plaintiff has no right, title and interest in the suit property. The learned Subordinate Judge, on hearing both the sides and considering evidence adduced by the parties decreed the suit on contest on 30-4-1987 declaring plaintiffs title to the suit land. Against the said Judgment and decree the contesting defendant No. 2 filed an appeal, which was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, Pabna. The appellate Court on hearing both the sides allowed the appeal of the defendant No. 2 and reversed the judgment passed by the trial Court and consequently the original suit stood dismissed by his judgment dated 14-3-1996. 

 4. The learned Senior Advocate Mr Rowshan Ali, appearing on behalf of the petitioner (plaintiff), has taken me through the judgments of both the courts below and the evidence on record. He submits that since the issue Nos. 2-3 relating to maintainability and limitation of the suit were not agitated before the trial Court, the appellate Court wrongly reopened the matters out of the way and took wrong decisions in respect of those issues uncalled for. It is submitted that the claim of the plaintiff is based on CS Khatian, which has got presumptive value as to its correctness but the learned Additional District Judge, discarded the said document at the instance of fictitious story introduced by the defendant No. 2 after a long span of time. That the defendant No. 2 never challenged the CS Khatian at any point of time in assertion of their interest. He submits that the defendant No. 2 also brought two conflicting stories of acquiring interest in the suit land, one from the alleged purchase from some fictitious co-sharers in the year 1968 and another by way of taking settlement from the Government admitting that he had no independent title in the land. It is further submitted that when the collusive auction sale was set aside, the ex-landlord or the successor Government did not acquire any interest in the said auction sale to hold its management and give settlement of the plaintiff's suit land. He has made further submission supporting the findings and decisions arrived at by the trial Court. It is submitted that the plaintiff petitioners, being the heirs of the original admitted owners, are in physical possession having title therein and they will suffer irreparable loss and injury if the impugned judgment and decree of the appellate Court are not set aside. 

 6. Admittedly, the suit land measuring 3.37 acres of land (Ga-Schedule including some other lands were recorded in the names of 3 sisters namely, Golejan Bibi, Rupjan Bibi and Sukjan Bibi in equal shares during Cadastral Survey (CS Operation). Exhibit 5 CC Khatian No. 56 stands in support of the contentions as to the previous ownership of the suit land according to the plaintiff's case, Sale Certificate dated 12-1-1954 (Boinama) submitted by the defendant in connection with Rent Execution Case No. 720 of 1953 filed by the ex-landlord Raja Protiva Nath Roy Bahadur against the original plaintiff Karimon Nessa and another CS recorded owner Golejan Bibi (her Khala). It indicates clearly that said plaintiff Karimon Nessa was the owner of the suit land with Golejan Bibi in the year 1953-54 when the auction sale was held. None of the defendant No. 2's predecessors, according to his genealogy given in the written statement, was party to the execution proceedings of the connected Rent suit which he relied on. Had they any interest and possession in the suit land according to the defendant's case, their names ought to have appeared amongst the defaulter tenants against whom auction proceeding was initiated. The defendant No. 2 though set up a separate case stating genealogy of Kichir Mondal, father of the CS recorded tenants as previous owner, he has not been able to establish such contention by substantial evidence in view of consistency in the plaintiffs clear case on the basis of CS Khatian. So, the defendant's case so far his claim of independent ownership through reversion heirs of Kichir Mondal, cannot be acceptable. Further, it is evident that actually the case of the defendant stands on the second contention ie termination of plaintiffs tenancy right, in the suit land on the basis of auction purchase by the ex-landlord Raja Protiva Nath Roy Bahadur. The defendant No. 2 relying on the auction sale submitted Bainanama dated 12-4-1954, which is Exhibit I. After the promulgation of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the suit land, alleged to have been auction purchased by the ex-landlord, vested in the Government as non-retainable Khas land. So, the defendant No. 2 prayed that the suit land was correctly recorded in the name of the Government during SA operation giving a complete go-by to his earlier stand of independent claim of title. Accordingly, the defendant No. 2 took lease from the Government vide Exhibit 3 which shows that the lease was given showing the suit land as khas land of the Government in the year 1974. In such view of the matter, it must be held that the CS Khatian can be taken as the basis of asserting ownership of the suit land and the plaintiff Karimon Nessa was admitted to be owner of the suit land as she was shown as judgment debtor of the Execution Case through which the admitted auction sale took place on 21-11-1953. 

 7. Thus, it appears that if the auction sale on the basis of Exhibit 1 stands good, then the defendant No. 2 has a defendable case of claiming possessor right on the basis of lease deed executed by the Government treating the suit land as non-retainable khas case land of the ex-landlord. In other words, if the SA Khatian is found to be correct, then only the defendant No. 2 is entitled to effectively resist the claim of the plaintiff as a leaseholder under the Government, otherwise not. Exhibit 3 is the Certified Copy of a petition filed by the plaintiff on 2-2-1959 under section 174(3) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1849 for setting aside the auction sale, which was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 26 of 1959 against the decree holder ex-landlord who was replaced by the Government, alleging that the auction was held in a fraudulent manner by suppressing notice on the plaintiff who was in physical possession. It appears that from Exhibit 4 that the said Miscellaneous Case was allowed setting aside the auction sale by the learned Munsif on 23-5-1959 and the plaintiff also paid arrears rent to the Government vide challan dated 17-4-1959 which is marked as Exhibit 2. In view of the order setting aside the prior auction sale in respect of the suit land, the plaintiffs title and possession cannot be said to have been terminated. Had she not been in physical possession, the application for setting aside the auction sale need not have been brought by her in the year 1959. It may be mentioned here that the decree holder auction purchaser did not take delivery of possession in the suit land in pursuance of the said auction sale, which had been subsequently set aside by the competent Court. No writ of delivery of possession is available. So, there is no reason to record the disputed land in the name of the Government as Khas land during SA Operation which was done after setting aside the auction sale in the year 1959. It is therefore, apparently a wrong record of right and the said Khatian in respect of the suit land ought to have been recorded in the name of original plaintiff Most. Karimon Nessa. So, the petitioners being admitted heirs of Karimon Nessa appear to have acquired good title in the suit land by way of inheritance. So far possession in the suit land is concerned, the plaintiff's side produced some Government dakhilas (Exhibit 1 series) and adduced 5 witnesses. They also paid arrear rent by a challan (Exhibit 2). All the PWs gave testimony in support of the plaintiffs possession, whereas 4 DWs said about possession of both the parties in the suit land. So, the assertion of plaintiffs possession gets affirmation by many DWs at least in respect of some portion of the suit land. The learned trial Court appears to have elaborately discussed evidence of possession and arrived at a proper finding in support of the plaintiff's possession. The appellate Court appears to have taken erroneous view in the matter of ascertaining possession due to misreading and non-consideration of material evidence on record, which I have already discussed above. 

 8. Mere knowledge about wrong recording of SA Khatian does not give rise to the cause of action to bring any suit, if the plaintiff does not bring such cause of action in the plaint. Limitation shall start running from the date of given cause of action. The learned Additional District Judge, Pabna, appears to have taken a wrong view in holding that since the plaintiff knew about the alleged wrong SA Khatian at the time of filing the suit bearing No. 410 of 1968 the present suit filed in the year 1975 was barred by limitation. He did not see that the plaintiffs cause of action in the present suit arose on 10-4-1975, when she came to know about the lease granted in favour of the defendant No. 2 by the Government. It appears from the lease deed that it was executed and registered on 16-7-1974. So, the plaintiff appears to have filed the suit in time from given cause of action and, as such, the suit cannot be said to have been barred by limitation under Article 120 of the Limitation Act. I have carefully gone through the judgment passed by the appellate Court along with the evidence on record and it is evident that the learned Additional District Judge has failed in error in taking decision in the appeal reversing the findings of the trial Court on the main question of acquisition of title and possession in the suit land. When some of the PWs admitted possession of the plaintiffs in some portion of the suit land, the learned Additional District Judge was totally wrong to find that the suit was not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Moreover, the findings arrived at by the learned trial Court on the question of possession appears to be sound and proper. Therefore, I hold the view that the findings and decision arrived at by the trial Court were not liable to be set aside in the appeal.

parties:
Taiyaba Zaman ----- Petitioner 
Vs.
Gias Uddin Ahmed and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the defendant-petitioner was issued directing the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the order 12-2-2002 passed by the learned Assistant Judge ,6th Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 137 of 2001 should not be set aside and such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. The short facts for disposal of the Rule are that, opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 137 of 2001 in the Court of Assistant Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka for declaration of his possessory right on the basis of Salami-purchase of the suit shop stating, in short, that one Jamal Ahmed Nomani was the original owner of the suit shop who transferred the possession of the said shop to one Mr Matiur Rahman (defendant No. 3) and that subsequently defendant No.3 having been in possession of the said shop through his tenant defendant No. 2 agreed to sell the same to the plaintiff and accordingly defendant No.3 sold his possession in the suit shop along with the furniture's of the shop to the plaintiff for a consideration of Taka 2,800 vide a written instrument dated 29-7-69 and that subsequently the plaintiff again paid Taka 3000 as fee of the transfer to the defendant No. 3 and since then the plaintiff has been in possession of the suit shop by paying rent regularly to the defendant No. 3 and further his case is that, he paid another Taka 2,000 to the defendant No. 3 for another room on 12-3-70 and thus the plaintiff is in possession of the suit shops by running a business under the name and style "Ms Famous Tailoring House." The further case of the plaintiff is that due to negotiation subsequently, a portion of the suit land (3 feet in breadth from the eastern portion of the property) was vacated and the rent was refixed to Taka 110 in place of Taka 135 per month and that subsequently as per direction of the defendant No.2 the plaintiff paid rent to the defendant No.1 (who is the present petitioner) and that subsequently again, the rent was refixed at Taka 85 in place of Taka 110 and he has been paying the same to the defendant No. 1 and that subsequently when he went to pay the rent for the month of May, 1988 the defendant No. 1 refused to accept the same and that similarly, the defendant No. 1 refused to receive the rent for the month of November, 1989 for which he filed House Rent Case No. 62 of 1989 and that the defendant No. I subsequently being annoyed started conspiracy to dispossess the plaintiff from the shop rooms and that subsequently the defendant No. 1 filed a suit for ejectment of the plaintiff being Small Causes Court Suit No.6 of 2000 on 5-11-2000 in the 6th Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka, and that cloud has been created in the title of the plaintiff regarding his possessory right so he filed the present suit showing cause of action on 5-11-2002. 

 3. The defendant petitioner contested the same suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations of the plaint and stating, inter alia, that the plaintiff being defaulter in payment of monthly rent the defendant filed Small Cause Court Suit No. 6 of 2000 for his ejectment and that the defendant or her predecessor never sold the possession of the suit shop to the plaintiff in any way and that the plaintiff is a habitual defaulter in payment of rent and that the defendant also requires the suit premises bonafide for constructing a building thereon. Further case of the defendant is that, the plaintiff filed similar suit being Title Suit No. 228 of 1997 in the same Court of the learned Assistant Judge (6th Court) on self- same allegations and reliefs which was ultimately dismissed for default and his Miscellaneous Case under Order IX rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure was allowed on condition to pay Taka 200 as cost. But the plaintiff having failed to deposit the cost of said Miscellaneous Case it was dismissed. 

 7. Mr Md Ibrahim Mollah, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant petitioner, placed the revisional application, the annexures, and the impugned order. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submitted that on the self-same allegations and reliefs the plaintiff having filed earlier Title Suit No. 228 of 1997 which was dismissed and subsequent Miscellaneous Case No. 46 of 1998 for restoration of the earlier suit having been dismissed for non-compliance of the Court's order for payment of cost; and the plaintiff having not taken any step further against that ex parte dismissal order as well as the order passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 46 of 1998, the present suit on the self-same allegations is not maintainable and the learned trial Court committed an error in rejecting the application. The learned Advocate further submitted that after dismissal of the aforesaid earlier Title Suit and Miscellaneous Case, the plaintiff having come to know about filing of the Small Cause Court Suit No. 6 of 2000 by the defendant-petitioner for ejectment of the plaintiff, he filed the present suit i.e. second suit, was the selfsame allegations only to defeat and delay the disposal of the ejectment suit and the learned trial Court without considering properly the facts and circumstances of the case committed an error in rejecting the application for rejection of the plaint. The learned Advocate further referring to Order IX rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure submitted that the plaintiff being precluded for bringing a fresh suit in respect of the same cause of action he brought the fresh suit on the same pleadings for the same reliefs on giving a different cause of action having no basis of substance to substantiate the same but only for the purpose of overriding or surpassing the law and the learned trial Court committed an error in rejecting the application for rejection of the plaint without considering this aspect of the case. 

 11. On a close reading of the said provision it clearly shows that in such circumstances a fresh suit in respect of the same cause of action is not maintainable but apparently there is no bar in bringing a fresh suit on a different cause of action and admittedly the present suit has been brought by showing a different cause of action. According to the learned Advocate of the petitioner, only because a different cause of action has been shown or given where the allegations, parties, reliefs and the suit land in both the suits being same, the present suit is not maintainable. In support of his submission the learned Advocate for the petitioner has referred to the decision in the case of Kumar Begum Roy vs Panna Debi and others reported in 1982 BLD (AD) 54, wherein similar question arose, that is, in the said reported case the plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 1508 of 1944 in the original side of Calcutte High Court claiming her title in the property of her husband and the said suit of the plaintiff having been dismissed for default on 1-9-49 the said plaintiff subsequently filed Title Suit No. 46 of 1961 (in this country) on the same allegation praying for the same relief against the same defendants and on objection by the defendants the trial Court dismissed the suit as being barred under Order IX rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure. On appeal the High Court Division upheld the trial Court's decision. Then there was an appeal before the Appellate Division. Their Lordships in the said decision held as follows: 

 "5 It appears from a reading of the plaint in Suit No. 1508/44 filed in the original side of the Calcutte High Court that the appellant claimed title to the property of deceased Naresh Narayan Roy on the basis of the marriage to him and conversion of the husband to Islam. There she prayed for the declaration of her right to the property of her late husband. In the plaint of the present suit the appellant has prayed for the declaration of her legal character and status as to the sole heir to the Estate left by her late husband who is the same person. If she obtains the declaration her right to the property in question would be established which she wanted to establish in the previous suit. By filing the present suit the appellant has merely adopted an indirect method to achieve the same result as she wanted to achieve in her suit filed in the Calcutta High Court. What she failed to scheme directly, she now wants to achieve indirectly. Law does not allow it to be done. It also appears that in the Calcutte High Court she did not proceed with the suit which was allowed to be dismissed for default on account of her non-appearance as she did not take any further step to have the orders of dismissal for default set aside. Under the provisions of Order IX, rule 9 CPC the present suit is barred." 

 12. The learned Advocate for the opposite party, on the other hand, has referred to the decision in the case of Haji Abdul Latif vs Abdul Huq and others reported in 44 DLR 601, in support of her submission that if the cause of action is different from that of the earlier suit then the second suit is maintainable. Ongoing through the said decision it appears that two suits were filed by the same plaintiff against the same defendants relating to the same land with the same relief, i.e. for permanent injunction. One suit was numbered as Title Suit No. 210 of 1981, another was numbered as Title Suit No. 188 of 1982 and both the suits proceeded at the same time and in both the suits the cause of action was same. The first suit having been dismissed the second suit continued. The defendants in the second suit then filed an application for rejection of the plaint of the second suit stating that on the same pleadings, the cause of action, the suit land, and the parties being same the second suit is barred. The learned trial Court while rejecting suit prayer of the defendant held that the second suit is not barred by any law, against which the defendant moved a revisional application before the High Court Division. In the said decision it has been held that the later suit having been brought before the dismissal of the 1st suit being Title Suit No. 210 of 1981, the bar of Order IX rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure has no manner of application in the present case. The distinguishing feature of this decision is that, both the suits were pending at the same time, between the same parties and relating to the same land, in other words, the later suit was not filed after the dismissal of the first suit. So, the cited decision is not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case where the later suit has been brought after dismissal of the first suit. The learned Advocate for the opposite party also submitted that "ie decision reported in 1982 BLD (AD) 54 is not applicable in the present case inasmuch as in the said decision nothing has been said about the cause of action that arose in two suits whether it was the same or different. 

 16. In the result, the Rule is made absolute and the impugned order dated 12-2-2002 passed in Title Suit No. 137 of 2001 is set aside and the application filed by the defendant for rejection of the plaint is allowed. Consequently the plaint of Title Suit No. 137 of 2001 is rejected and the suit is accordingly, dismissed, however without any order as to cost.

parties:
Zillul Haq and others ------ Petitioners
Vs. 
Maloti Bala Dey and ors ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the Judgment and decree dated 12-9-1996 passed by the Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Sylhet in Title Appeal No.4 of 1996 reversing the judgment and decree dated 27-11-1995 passed by the Assistant Judge, Gowainghat, Sylhet in Title Suit No. 174 of 1992. Malati Bala Dey, mother of opposite party No.1 (Ka), as plaintiff instituted a suit in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Sylhet being Title Suit No.151 of 1977, subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No. 174 of 1992 on transfer to the Court of Assistant Judge, Sylhet praying for a declaration that the orders dated 13-11-1976 and 16-4-1977 passed in Miscellaneous Case No.20 of 1976 by the ADC (Revenue), Sylhet are illegal and without jurisdiction and also for a permanent injunction restraining the defendant-opposite parties from interfering with her peaceful possession in the suit property. 

 2. The plaintiff''''s case, in short, is that, except the land covered by Khatian Nos. 399 and 445 the remaining portion of the suit property belonged to Binode Bihari Das who owned and possessed the same. It was further contended that the suit land was the self-acquired property of Binod Bihari Das. The land of Khatian Nos. 399 and 445 was the ancestral property of the said Binode Bihari Das who had two other full-brothers, namely, Birendre Kumar Das and Bimala Charan Das and the three brothers jointly owned and possessed the same. While being in exclusive possession in the suit property the said Binode Behari Das executed a registered will in favour of the plaintiff in respect of the suit land. Subsequently, the said Binode Behari died in this country in 1962 as a citizen of the erstwhile Pakistan and since his death the plaintiff has been owning and possessing the suit property peacefully on payment of rent to the Govt. Acquired Estate. It was further contended that the aforesaid will executed by Binode Bihari Das has been duly probated by a competent civil Court and she duly obtained letters of Administration against the said will. The defendants illegally served a notice on her in the later part of 1976 asking her to surrender possession of the suit property as vested property. She thereafter filed an application before the ADC (Rev), Sylhet praying for cancellation of the aforesaid notice but to no effect. It was further contended that as far back as in the year 1972 the matter was taken up for investigation by the Sub-Divisional Officer, who after due enquiry into the matter found that the suit property is not a vested property. The plaintiff contended that she has title and possession in the suit property and, as such, the defendants have no right to disturb her lawful possession by exercising executive powers. 

 4. Added defendant Nos, 13-23, claiming to be yearly lessees under the Government, also filed written statement supporting the case of the principal defendants contending, inter alia, that after taking the lease from the Government they have been possessing the suit land along with others and the plaintiff has no title and possession in the suit property and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 6. The learned Assistant Judge by the impugned judgment dated 21-11-1995 dismissed the suit on contest. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree, the plaintiff preferred an appeal before the District Judge, Sylhet being Title Appeal No.4 of 1996, and the First Additional District Judge, who heard the appeal, has been pleased by the impugned judgment dated 12-5-1996 to reverse the judgment of the trial Court and decreed the suit. 

 9. Mr. Idrisur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of added opposite party Nos.42-43, who are alleged to have purchased the suit property from the original plaintiff during the pendency of the suit, sups arts the judgment of the Court of appeal below and submits that the learned Additional District Judge on proper consideration of the evidence on record was perfectly justified in reversing the judgment of the trial Court assigning cogent reasons and the same has occasioned no failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that in view of the admitted fact that the original plaintiff has title, at least in some portion of the suit property and admittedly the plaintiff has possession in the suit property, the Government has no right to physically oust her from possession by exercising executive powers except in due course of law and, as such, the learned Additional District Judge committed no error of law in passing the decree for permanent injunction. 

 10. I have carefully gone through the impugned judgment passed by the learned Court of appeal below. It appears that the learned Additional District Judge on detailed discussion of al, evidence of seven PWs and two PWs found that the plaintiff is in rightful possession of the suit property and the Government has not as yet taken over possession of the suit property. The learned Court of appeal below further found that the plaintiff has interest at least in some portion of the suit property on the basis of the will duly executed by Binode Bihari Das in her favour as far back as in 1962 and she has rightful possession in the suit property on the basis of the Letters of Administration duly granted by a competent civil Court. The learned Additional District Judge further found that the plaintiff's possession in the suit property being admitted and it being not unlawful and unauthorised she is entitled to protection of her lawful possession against executive high handedness. The learned Court of appeal below further found that although she is not the owner of the entire suit property still she is not liable to be evicted there from except in due course of law by persons having interests in the disputed property. It appears that the learned Additional District Judge reversed the material findings of the trial Court on proper consideration of the evidence on record on assigning cogent reasons in support of his conclusions. 

 11. From the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record it is manifestly clear that the original plaintiff Sarala Bala possessed the suit property as an undivided joint property since the death of Binode Behari Das, one of the admitted recorded tenants, on the basis of a registered will duly executed by Binode Behari in her favour. It is not also disputed that the said will has duly been probated by a competent civil Court. Although the said will created definite interests in plaintiff Malati Rani in the suit property to the extent of interest of the share of Benode Behari she has not acquired interest in the entire suit property as two-thirds of the disputed property are evidently a vested property inasmuch as the admitted co-owners Birendra and Bimala Kanta left for India and became Indian nationals long ago and their shares in the suit property vested in the Govt. by operation of law. Plaintiff Malati Rani is thus found to be a co-sharer in possession of the ejmali suit property. 

 13. The learned Additional District Judge appears to have rightly addressed himself to this moot question and found that since the plaintiff's possession in the suit land cannot be termed as unlawful and she is admittedly in possession of the disputed property, she is entitled to a decree for permanent injunction. 

 17. The judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Sylhet in Title Appeal No. 4 of 1996 are affirmed.

caseno: Civil Petition for leave to appeal No. 376 of 1992
parties:
Akil Uddin Mallick and others ------ Defendant-Petitioners
Versus
Jonab Ali Sheikh ------ Plaintiff-Respondent.
full_judgment:
Mohammad Abdur Rouf, J:- This petition for leave to appeal, by the defendants, is from the Judgment and order dated 11.5.92 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1916 of 1981 making the Rule absolute and decreeing the suit after setting aside the judgment and decree dated 6.7.81 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Jhenidah in Title Appeal No. 22 of. 1980 dismissing the suit on reversal of the judgment and decree dated 11.5.79 passed by the learned Munsif, 2nd Court, Jhenidah in Title Suit no 407 of 1973 decreeing the suit. 

 2. Plaintiff-respondent No. 1 instituted the suit for declaration of title to 32 a decimals of land appertaining to 13 decimals of plot No. 19452, 13 decimals from plot No. 19368 and 06 1/2 decimals from plot No. 19397 of Mouza Taraf-Umedpur Plaintiffs case in short is that one Ketabdi Monde being the owner in possession settled the suit land with the plaintiffs mother, Orenja Nessa, on 14 Falgun, 1341 B.S. corresponding to 26.2.35 A.D. by a registered patta (Ext. 1) and since then the plaintiffs mother had been possessing the same. After her death the plaintiff inherited the same and has been in possession therein, Defendant No. 1 has been possessing the remaining portion of plot Nos. 19768. 19397. But the suit property has wrongly been recorded in S.A. Khatian No. 868 in the name of the defendants. 

 3. Defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the right, title and possession of the plaintiff in the suit land. His case in short is that the original tenancy right of Meher Molla and others in respect of the suit property was auction purchased by the landlord of Kashim Bazar Raj Estate in execution of a rent decree about 42 years back Defendant No. 1 in Magh. 1340 B.S. took settlement of the suit land from the said' landlord and since then he has been possessing the same. 

 4. The trial court on consideration of the oral evidence of 3 P.Ws and 4 D.Ws and the documentary evidence produced by the parties decreed the suit holding both title and possession of the plaintiff in the suit land. On appeal preferred by the defendants the lower appellate court 

 reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit holding, inter alia, that the plaintiff failed to prove exclusive possession of Ketab Ali, the plaintiffs mother in the suit land and that the plaintiffs document of title, the certified copy of the patta, Ext. I was not legally proved. In the revision the High Court Division held, inter alia, that the lower appellate court upon misreading of the evidence of P.Ws. 2 and 3 wrongly held that the plaintiff could not prove his possession in the suit land and that the lower appellate court also wrongly held that the plaintiffs document of title i.e. patta was not legally proved. 

 further submits that the High Court Division wrongly held that the certified copy of the original patta proved plaintiffs title to the disputed land while the lower appellate court in consideration of the other relevant facts rightly held that such certified copy was inadmissible in evidence. 

 6. The learned Judge of the High Court Division clearly noticed that the lower appellate court did not consider the entire oral evidence of P.Ws. 2 and 3 and misreading their evidence wrongly held that those two P.Ws supported the plaintiffs possession in only one of the suit plots viz plot NO. 19452 and that they remained silent as regards the plaintiffs possession in the other two plots. The High Court Division found that those two P.Ws specifically stated in their examinations-in-chief as well as in cross-examination that the plaintiff is in possession of the suit property. which is comprised of 32 a decimals of land in total in the three suit plots mentioned above. Non-consideration and misreading of material evidence of the P.Ws being a question of law the High Court Division was justified in setting aside the finding of possession against the plaintiff of the lower appellate court. The High Court Division also rightly repelled the second submission made by Mr. Abdur Rahim as regards the admissibility of Ext. 1, the certified copy of the relevant patta. It was marked as an exhibit without any objection by the defendants. The plaintiff in his evidence also explained the reason for his failure to produce the original patta
justice_names: Mr. Justice Bimalendu Bikash Roy Chowdhury
case_type_name: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal

caseno:
Civil Revision No. 4646 of 1991 (Dhaka) 
Civil Revision No. 37 of 1990 (Comilla)
parties:
Harunur Rashid ------ Petitioner
vs. 
Zakiatun Nessa Begum & others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
2. Opposite party No. 1 Zakiatun Nessa Begum as plaintiff filed the aforesaid suit for declaring decree dated 26.11.79 passed in TS No. 152 of 1974 as fraudulent, collusive and void on the allegation that petitioner and opposite party No. 2 filed Title Suit No. 152 of 1974 in the Court of the Munsif, Cox's Bazar against plaintiffs' father Ezaharul Huq and after his death on 17.5.76 all his heirs except defendant opposite party No. 12 Jashimuddin were substituted on 2.6.76 and defendant opposite party No. 10 Enamul Huq was shown as major though he was minor at that time and plaintiff was substituted as minor Jaikkani and the plaintiff after attaining majority came to know that no Court guardian was appointed for the minor defendants of that suit and her mother, an illiterate Pardanashin woman, was shown as their natural guardian. Her further case is that her elder brothers making show of contest on behalf of all the heirs allowed the said suit to be decreed in favour of the petitioner and opposite party No. 2 and had that suit been properly contested the same could not have been decreed on 26.11.79 and thereafter petitioner and opposite party No. 2 obtained an ex parte decree in a money suit against the opposite party Nos. 1 and 3-11 and quarrel ensued between the brothers over the same and at that time on 1.8.85 plaintiff opposite party No. 1 came to know about the decree in Title Suit No. 152 of 1974. 

 5. It appears from the judgment of the trial Court that Court guardian was appointed on behalf of the minor defendants of Title Suit No. 152 of 1972 and he did not contest the suit on behalf of the minors as in the meantime all the substituted defendants submitted joint written statement and natural guardian Safura Khatun defendant No. 1 (Niya) signed the same on behalf of the minors as natural guardian and the suit was decreed on contest and trial Court did not believe plaintiffs story of strained relationship with her brothers and further found that they had good relationship and also found that the plaintiff contested the said suit through her Advocate and the plaintiff and other defendants of that suit had no conflicting interest and the plaintiff was aware of that suit. Court of appeal below, on the other hand, found that plaintiffs mother Safura Khatun and her brother Jashimuddin were not substituted in Title Suit No. 152 of 1974 and, as such, that suit abated against them and defendant opposite party No. 10 Enamul Huq was minor at that time but he was shown as major and the plaintiff was substituted as minor Jaikkani Khatun though her actual name is Jakitunnessa Begum and therefore Court of appeal below found that decree passed in Title Suit 152 of 1974 was invalid for defect of parties, insufficient valuation and for preventing the minor defendants from contesting the suit. 

 6. It is not the case of the plaintiff in her plaint that her mother Safura Khatun was not substituted in the earlier suit. In spite of that, Court of appeal below unnecessarily came to the finding that she was not substituted relying upon some mistake in the record of Title Suit No. 152 of 1974 overlooking that the said Safura Khatun contested the suit after substitution as defendant No.1 (Niya) by filing joint written statement along with other heirs of deceased defendant Ezaharul Huq. When it was neither the case of Safura Khatun nor her daughter plaintiff that she was not substituted in that suit I find the aforesaid finding of the Court of appeal below is illegal and without any basis. 

 7. Ezaharul Huq, original defendant of Title Suit No. 152 of 1974 died on 17.5.76 and his heirs were substituted in that suit on 2.6.76 as defendant Nos. 1 (ka) to 1 (niya). Court of appeal below inferred that defendant opposite party No.l2 was born within 10 months of the death of his father on 17.5.76. There is no positive evidence on record when Jasimuddin was born. Petitioner stated that at the time of filing the substitution petition said Jashimuddin was not born. So I fail to understand how he could have been substituted in the earlier suit on 2.6.76 when he was not born. In the case of Mohd Sulaiman vs. Mohd Ismail reported in AIR 1966 (SC) 792 in paragraph 5 it has been held as follows: 

 8. Purpose of substitution of the heirs of a deceased plaintiff or defendant is to represent the estate of the deceased party in the proceedings. If some of the heirs of the deceased plaintiff or defendant are substituted and they appear in the suit or proceedings and without taking any objection about non-substitution of other heirs of the deceased party goes on proceeding with or contesting the suit that cannot make the decree passed ultimately in the suit nugatory or illegal for want of non-substitution of some of the heirs simply because the estate of the deceased plaintiff or defendant was well represented in the proceedings by substitution of some of the heirs whose names were known to the other party. In the instant case all the heirs of deceased defendant Ezaharul Hoq were substituted as defendant Nos. 1 (ka) to 1 (niya) in Title Suit No. 152 of 1974 within the period of limitation and defendant opposite party No. 12 Jashimuddin was not born at that time. Merely because the name of the plaintiff was written incorrectly in the substitution petition or defendant opposite party No. 10 Enamul Hoque was shown as major instead of minor contested decree in that suit against all the substituted heirs of Ezaharul Huq cannot be said to be illegal or void especially when natural guardian mother contested on behalf of all the minors. It is also now well settled that non- substitution of some of the heirs whose names could not be gathered in spite of due diligence or an heir not born at the time of substitution cannot make the decree ultimately passed in the suit illegal or void. 

 9. Court of appeal below unnecessarily ventured to find fault with insufficient valuation of the earlier suit, failure of the Court guardian to file written statement on behalf of minor defendants or validity of the delivery of possession of the suit property in favour of the petitioner and opposite party No. 2 in Title Execution Case No. 118 of 1980 though the same were beyond the scope of the present suit. Entire impugned judgment shows either lack of judicial experience or extra-judicial consideration on the part of the Court of appeal below.

caseno: Civil Revision Nos. 1086 of 1992 with 1087 of 1992
parties:
Shankar Chandra Das and others ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Kalachand Das ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
2. This Rule at the instance of the plaintiff-appellant petitioners was directed against the judgment and decree dated 16.4.94 and 22.4.92 respectively passed by the Subordinate Judge, Commercial Court, Barisal in Title Appeal No. 115 of 1990 affirming the judgment and decree dated 26.5.90 and 6.6.90 respectively passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Barisal in Title Suit No. 395 of 1984. 

 Babu Tufan Das, the predecessor of the plaintiff appellant-petitioner being plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 235 of 1981 in the Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge) 2nd court at Barisal against the defendant-opposite party for khan possession by evicting the defendant from the suit but as described in the schedule to the plaint and subsequently on transfer of the suit to the court of Senior Assistant Judge, Barisal, it was renumbered as Title Suit No. 395 of 1984. The case of the plaintiff is that the plaintiff is the owner of 0.09 decimal of land of RS plot No. 2048 by pattan taken in 1359 BS from the previous owner Sukumar Sen and others. This land was wrongly recorded in the khatian in the name of the previous owner and so, the plaintiff Tufan Das filed a suit being Title Suit No. 555 of 1958 against the said previous owner for declaration of this title in the suit land and the suit was decreed on 15.7.59 and then the plaintiff Tufan Das got his name recorded in the khatian and paid rent and taxes as usual and thus the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land. That the defendant opposite party No. 1 is the younger brother of the plaintiff and that the defendant had no house of his own in the town and on his prayer, the plaintiff allowed the defendant to stay in the northern bhiti Gulpata hut measuring 8 x 5 Banga in 1976 and since then the defendant has been residing therein temporarily in the suit hut. That subsequently plaintiff petitioner wanted to make a pucca construction on his own land and for that purpose the plaintiff asked the defendant opposite party to vacate his Gulpata hut but that the defendant refused to vacate the hut and, as such, the plaintiff-petitioner instituted the aforesaid title suit for khas possession. 

 4. After 5 years of plaintiffs Title Suit No. 235 of 1981(renumbered as Title Suit No. 395 of 1984), the defendant-opposite party as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 19 of 1986 against this petitioner as defendant for declaration of his title in 8 annas share of the total suit property of 0.09 decimals of land and also for a declaration that the decree dated 15.7.59 passed in Title Suit No. 555 of 1958 is fraudulent, collusive, void and not binding upon the opposite party. The claim of the opposite party in his Title Suit No. 19 of 1986 is that the petitioner and the opposite party being full-brothers and that the petitioner being the eldest brother, both of them jointly took settlement of the disputed land from the previous owner but that the petitioner fraudulently instituted Title Suit No. 555 of 1958 claiming his sole interest in the land in question and obtained a fraudulent collusive decree on 15.7.59. The learned Assistant Judge held analogous trial of both the suits and decided both the suits by one judgment. After hearing the parties, the learned Assistant Judge, dismissed the suit for eviction brought by the plaintiff-petitioner and decreed the suit of the opposite party for declaration of his title in 8 annas share vide his judgment and decree dated 26.5.90 and 6.6.90 respectively. 

 7. Mr. Shamsul Alam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant-petitioners, has submitted that the opposite party failed to prove his case of joint settlement in his Title Suit No. 19 of 1986 and that he could not also prove by any evidence that he took the settlement of the suit land along with his brother the petitioner but that both the courts below by misreading the facts and evidence, decided both the suits in favour of the opposite party and thus this decision of the learned Subordinate Judge has caused a failure of justice to the plaintiff-petitioners. 

 9. By a perusal of the impugned judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge, it appears that the plaintiff petitioner's case is that he alone took settlement of 0.09 decimal of land of plot No. 1533 of CS Khatian No. 859 from the original owner Kiran Bala Das and others in 1359 BS but defendant opposite party's case, on the other hand, was that Kiran and others granted settlement of this 0.09 decimal of land to both Tufan Das and Kala Chand Das in 13th Falgoon 1359 BS but that none of the parties filed any paper to show the claim of the respective settlement. From this fact it appears that the alleged settlement was an oral settlement and, as such, that was a matter for decision by oral evidence. 

 11. Mr. Shamsul Alam, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioners, submits that the plaintiff-petitioner subsequently filed a Title Suit No. 555 of 1958 against the original owner and got the decree and then got his name recorded in SA Khatian by filing Misc. Case under section 54 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and then paid rent to the Government regularly and that all these papers have been marked as exhibits in the suit but that the learned courts below did not consider these facts of the case. 

 12. In this respect, Mr. Mihir Kanti Majumder, the learned Advocate for the opposite party, has contended that these are the subsequent papers and that these papers and the rent receipts cannot create any title in favour of the plaintiff- petitioner, nor can it take away the defendant opposite party's right, title from the suit land. 

 13. It appears that the learned trial Court have discussed the facts of the case more elaborately with reference to the evidence and the legal presumption and came to the finding that both the brothers took settlement and both of them paid salami money of Taka six hundred to the landlord by selling that paternal land to Halima Khatun. The trial Court further found from the evidence of PWs and DWs that both brothers, Tufan Das and Kala Chand Das have been living in the suit property in their respective separate huts since 37/38 years with their family and that the decree obtained by Tufan Das in Title Suit No. 555 of 1958 was an ex parte and collusive decree and this had been done by elder brother Tufan Das to deprive the younger brother Kala Chand Das from the suit property. The learned Subordinate Judge also came to the conclusion that the learned trial Court has rightly come to this decision. 

 "The suit being one for declaration of title to an unspecified share of an undivided plot of land on the basis of gift and there being no evidence that the donor thereof was in exclusive possession at any time is not maintainable without a prayer for partition." 

 15. Mr. Mihir Kanti Majumder, the learned Advocate for the opposite party, in this respect argued that the case referred to above was a case, for declaration of title filed by the plaintiff on the basis of a transfer by gift and that his donor's exclusive possession therein was not proved at all, but that the instant case before us is not a case of title on the basis of purchase of gift but that it is a case of original co-ownership and the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 19 of 1986 is admittedly in joint possession of the suit property and, as such, the nature of the present case is quite different from the case referred to above. In this connection, Mr. Mihir Kanti Majumder referred to a decision in the case of Joy Narain Sen Ukil Vs. Srikanta and others reported in AIR 1922 (Cal) 8 wherein it has been held that: 

 "Where a plaintiff is in joint possession of immovable property, whether such possession be actual possession of his share of the whole or actual possession of part coupled with constructive possession of the remainder, he is entitled to maintain a suit for declaratory relief with a view to remove a cloud on his title created by the act of the defendant disputing his share; in a suit so framed declaration of title is all that plaintiff needs and he is consequently not called upon to ask for consequential relief by way of partition." 

 Mr. Mihir Kanti Majumder argued that it has been established by evidence that the opposite party is a co-owner in joint possession of the suit property comprising 0.09 decimal of land and, as such, the suit in the form of declaration of his title in respect of his share in this 0.09 decimal being clouded by his brother will be maintainable. 

 16. It appears that in the instant case the opposite party being plaintiff filed his Title Suit No. 19 of 1986 for simple declaration of title in respect of 8 anna share in the suit property comprising 0.09 decimal of land. Admittedly, the total suit land is 0.09 decimal and both the brothers are jointly living therein, therefore, it is not an unspecified land but that it is quite a specified piece of 0.09 decimal of land, part of which is in exclusive physical possession of the younger brother since 37/38 years as has been found by both the courts below. So, in the facts and circumstances of the instant case before us, the principle laid down in the cited case of AIR, 1922 (Cal) at page 8 appears to be applicable. I, therefore, find that the defendant's case being suit No. 19 of 1986 will be maintainable in this form and that the learned courts below have correctly come to their conclusion. 

 "Rent receipts are evidence of possession, and may be used as collateral evidence of title. Mr Alam contends that the plaintiff petitioner paid rent of the suit land to the government and received dakhil as which are exhibit 8 series but that the defendant opposite party could not produce a piece of dakhila showing his payment of any rent or taxes. Mr. Alam argued that these rent receipts have presumptive value towards the petitioner's possession and title in whole of the suit property. 

 Admittedly, the petitioner and the opposite party of the instant case are two brothers. Admittedly, both the brothers are living in the suitland of 0.09 decimal of land in two separate huts on the basis of a pattan from the original owners. Both the courts below discussed all the facts, circumstances and the evidences on record quite elaborately and correctly together with presumptive circumstances of the case and came to a concurrent finding of fact that both the brothers have been living in this 0.09 decimals of land in their respective separate huts since 1359 BS entering therein at a time and thus the learned courts found that both the brothers have got title and possession in the suit property. I do not find any misreading or mis-appreciation of the evidence by any of the courts below. I find that the learned Subordinate Judge has correctly and properly discussed and appreciated the facts, circumstances and the evidence of both the cases and come to the conclusion on the basis of the materials on record. I do not find anything wrong in his finding of facts.

caseno: Appeal from Original decree No. 76 of 1963.
parties:
Padmabati Biswas ------ Appellants 
Vs. 
Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Badrul Islam Chowdhury, J. : This appeal at the instance of defendant Nos. 24 and 31-38 arises out of the judgment and decree dated 19.4.62 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Khulna in Title Suit No. 5 of 1959. 

 2. Collector of Khulna on 16.5.59 made a reference to the Alluvial Lands Act, 1920 stating that some island chars were formed in the bed of the river Kazibacha in Mouza Tetultala within PS Batiaghata in the District of Khulna, as depicted in the sketch-map attached to the letter of reference, which had been shown as blocks 1-5 and 6-7 as prepared by khas mahals Surveyor and the chars comprising of 129.22 acres of cultivable land were being claimed by different persons including the government with the result that there were occasions for breach of peace. It was further stated that the Collector of Khulna therefore, attached the said char land in accordance with the provision of section 3 of the aforesaid Act and had appointed District Manager as receiver for management of the said land. The land were still under attachment and in possession of the receiver. As the Collector thought that rival claims of title and possession of this char land were likely to cause further breach of peace he referred the matter to the District Judge, Khulna for determining the claims of the different claimants. The District Judge under sub-section (2) of section 5 of the said Act transferred the reference to the Court of Subordinate Judge, Khulna where it was registered as Title Suit No. 5 of 1959. In the letter of reference 11 persons including the government were shown as persons claiming title and possession over the disputed land. However, after service of notice under section 5 of the said Act by the Court 40 more persons entered appearance and set up claims over the disputed land. They were added as defendant Nos. 12-51 in the suit. 

 4. Claimant Nos. 2-51 have been treated by the trial Court as defendants in the suit and for the sake of convenience we shall also term them as such. Defendant No. 2 Abdul Haque Sarder claims that during CS operation it was found that the river Kazibacha, which is also known as Ramdashia, flowed through Mouza Tetultala comprised in the permanent settlement estate of Touzi No. 120 of Khulna Collectorate and as such the settlement authority treated the former bed of the river as Diara land. Accordingly a Diara proceeding was started, and in the CS maps (sheet Nos. 1-3) prepared in 1922-23 this diara land was demarcated and a new Touzi No. 1144 was assigned to it. The land of these diara Touzi was taken in settlement by the proprietors of Touzi No. 120. The further case of defendant No. 2 is that river Kazibacha formerly flowed by the north-south and eastern sides of Mouza Tetultala but subsequently it receded on the north and south as a result of which there was gradual and imperceptible accretion to the land of Touzi Nos. 120 and 1140. In 1940 the Government again surveyed the land of Touzi No. 1140. Along with land accreted to this touzi were delineated in the map so prepared and separate khatians were opened in the names of those who were holding the land contiguous to their Asli land. But there was no survey of the land accreted to Touzi No. 120. However, the landlords brought suits against the tenants who were holding the land in Touzi No. 120 for increase of rent on the ground of accretion and the same were decreed. In or around 1942 one island char measuring 2.55 acres was formed out of the bed of the river opposite to CS Plot Nos. 51-54. A similar island char measuring 16.60 acres arose out of the bed of river Kazibacha. Both these island chars were surrounded on all sides by deep water of the river. Government under the provision of section 4 of Regulation No. XI/1825 claimed both the chars as khas land and the Collector of Khulna started Settlement Case No. 54/46-47, got both the chars surveyed and map prepared. Initially both these two chars, one situated to the south of the other, were allotted Touzi No. 1442 which was subsequently changed to Touzi No. 1444 under Khas Mahal Officer's Order dated 27.5.48. Defendant No. 2, Abdul Haque Sarder, Kali Kanta Chatterjee, Anil Kumar Ghosh and Bupendra Nath Das who were tenure holders under the aforesaid Touzi Nos. 120 and 1142 took permanent settlement in raiyati right of both the above mentioned island chars at a rental of rupees 3.00 per acre from the government on payment of salami and by executing 4 separate kabuliyats in the year 1946 AD. Kabuliyats were accepted by the government and the tenants paid rent. The kabuliyats contained the stipulation that in case of increment to the leased out island chars, the lessees would pay enhanced rent at the stipulated rate. Lessee Kali Kanta Chatterjee settled his share comprising 4.79 acres to defendant No. 3 Sk. Nuruddin by patta dated 10.2.48. Lessee Anil Kumar Ghosh sold his 4.79 acre to one Mahbubur Rahman who in turn settled 1.50 acres out of his purchased land with defendant Nos. 5-7 in 1354 BS at an annual rent at Rupees 7-8-0 annas and sold the remaining 3.29 acres as well as rent receiving interest of the settled 1.50 acres to defendant Nos. 5-7 by kabala dated 25.10.56. Bupendra Nath Das, the other lessee, sold his share to defendant No. 4 by kabala dated 20.12.48 while defendant No. 2 remained in possession of his share of leased land. Gradually further land accreted to the northern island char and defendant No. 2 began to possess that accreted land too. There are two khals or channels on the east and west of this char. Out of the land accreted to this char seven bighas was settled with Monsur Bawali and Sariatullah Sk. by patta dated 29.5.51 with an annual rent of Rupees 14-0-0 and they arc possessing that land. Defendant No. 2 is in possession of the landaccreted to this northern island char. Thus defendant No. 2 possessed 28.00 acres land including the tenanted land and Asli land of 2.55 acres of touzi No. 1444. He also possesses 2.23 acres on the eastern side of the southern char of touzi No. 1444 by virtue of his lease taken from the government and with gradual accretion to this land by the recess of the river he had been possessing the accreted land as well. Defendant No. 2 further alleges that before attachment of the land a proceeding under section 144 CrPC was started at the instance of the Khas Mahal Depart.ment wherein it was clearly admitted that the disputed land were accret.ion to touzi 120 and 1144 and the said proceeding was ultimately dropped. Defendant No. 2 further claims that before attachment by the Collect.or the char contiguous to CS Plot No. 3 was possessed by defendant No. 3 Dwarik Mondal who is korfatenant under one Nalini Bala Chatterjee who is an under-tenant under defendant No. 2, the tenure formed under CS Plot No. 47 was being possessed by successors of Bangeshwar Chatterjee; that the lands of block No. 1 of Collector's map was in possession of defendant No. 9 and sons of Bangeshwar; that the land accreted to CS Plot Nos. 8 and 9 was in possession of defendant No. 9 Rabia Khatun along with her co-sharers; the land accreted to CS Plot No. 101 was possessed by Upendra Nath Mondal and his co-sharers and these persons were tenants under defendant. No. 2 who realised additional rent for the additional areas; that one Zohura Khatun had been possessing CS Plots No. 113 and 115 of khatian No. 24 and portion of block Nos. 6 and 7 of Collector's map as accretion to her land by purchase from Satish Chandra Bhadra.
