 24. At the very outset we would like to dispose of the legal objection taken by the learned Deputy Attorney-General. Sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act as amended by PO Nos. 72, 135 and 137 of 1972 introduced radical changes in the century old law with respect to land gained by the recess of river or of the sea, as well as land reformed in situ, by providing that such accreted land or reformed land not be considered as the land of riparian or the original owner, as the case may be, but shall vest in the government free from all encumbrances, unless such accretion or reformation was finally recognised or declared by a competent authority or Court under any law for the time being in force. This provision of law was also given retrospective effect by insertion of the words "whether the loss of such land or portion by diluvion took or takes place before or after the commencement of State Acquisition &Tenancy (Fourth Amendment) Order, 1972. This fourth amendment is incorporated in PO 135 of 1972. In sub-section (3) similar provisions have been made with respect to land reformed in situ. Sub-section (5) of this amended section 86 further provides that all suits, applications, appeals or other proceeding with respect to any claim to the re-possession of any land lost by diluvion which has re-appeared or is alleged to have re-appeared pending before any Court or authority on the date of commencement of the said PO 135 of 1972 shall not proceed and shall abate. Mr. Moazzem Hossain relying on the provisions of this amended law as contained in sub-sections (2), (3) and (5) of section 86 contends that admittedly the disputed land are accretions as claimed by some of the defendants or reformation in situ as claimed by others and since the litigation with respect to title and possession over the said land was pending on the date of coming into force of PO 135 of 1972 the present appeal, which is a continuation of the original suit, cannot proceed and should abate. This contention of the learned Deputy Attorney-General may appear correct on the face of the provisions contained in statute itself. However, every law must be looked into not only by the language appearing in the statute book but also by its interpretation as enunciated by the superior courts of the country. Our Constitution enjoins that the decisions of the highest court i.e. the Supreme Court of Bangladesh should be followed and acted upon by all authorities and subordinate Courts. A decision given by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court is binding upon all Courts including the High Court Division. In the case of Abdul Mannan Vs. Kulada Ranjan Mowali reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195, their Lordships of the Appellate Division after discussing the history of the development of the law relating to accretion and reformation-in-situ as well as the provisions of sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act, 1950 as amended in 1972 have held: 

 26. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed has raised objection as regards the correctness of the sketch-map prepared by the Collector and appended to the letter of reference. We find that at the time of trial the District Kanungo of Khulna ABM Moslemuddin was examined as PW 1 on behalf of the government represented by the Collector of Khulna, He deposed to the effect that after attachment of the disputed land the Collector ordered for survey of the same and accordingly Amin Abdul Masud Chowdhury surveyed and then Kanungo Monjur Ali prepared the map. On perusal of the said map it appears that the revenue survey lines as well as the channels have been depicted therein. From Ext. I, it also appears that on the application of one Haran Chand Mallik the Collector of Khulna started Misc. Case. No. 54 of 1957 and in that case the map was prepared by the Government Surveyor. Moreover, on scrutiny of the sketch map it becomes crystal clear that it contains the entire land in dispute and it has been sufficiently identified. Moreover, the original two island chars, the accreted land, khals, revenue survey lines and all other salient features of the disputed property have been clearly depicted in the map. So we find that the learned Subordinate Judge rightly came to the finding that there was no defect in the sketch map relating to the disputed land prepared under the order of the Collector and appended to the letter of reference. The law relating to chars or alluvial land is laid down in the Bengal Alluvion and Diluvion Regulations, 1825 (Regulation No. XI of 1825). The first clause of section 4 of Regulation XI of 1825 provides: 

 Thus the law as it was in force at the relevant time provided that all alluvial land would be increment to the land of the Zaminder or tenant who held the main land under any superior landlord including the government. No doubt in the third clause it has been provided that if a char is thrown opened in a large navigable river the bed of which is not the property of any individual and if the channels of the river between the char and the main land are not fordable it shall be at the disposal of the government, but if the channel is fordable in any season of the year it shall be acquisition to the land of the persons whose estate may be most contiguous to it. Relying on this provision of law, the leaned Deputy Attorney-General Mr. Moazzem Hossain contends that it is admitted by almost all the contending parties in the suit that two island chars arose out of the bed of the river Kazibacha which was navigable at the relevant time and the two chars have been depicted as 'A' in the sketch map, in that view of the matter, according to him, these two chars belong to the government as per provision of clause (3) of section 4 of regulation XI of 1825 and any accretion to these two chars are accretion to government khas land and no one else can set forth claim over them. There is no doubt about the fact that PWs 1 and 2 as well as OWs 1-6 who were witnesses for defendant Nos. 2-7 in unequivocal language stated that in or around 1940 two island chars, one described as the northern char comprising of 2.55 acres, and the other as the southern char comprising 16.60 acres arose out of the bed of the river Kazibacha running through mouza Tetultala. DW 8 Mansur Bawali who is defendant No. 22, DW 9 Hatem Ahmed who deposed on behalf of defendant Nos. 9 and 12-18, DW 10 Tarek Mondal who deposed on behalf of defendant No. 21 also supported the case of the government and DWs 1-6 about the raising of these two chars out of the bed of the river which belonged to nobody. Therefore, there remains no doubt about the fact that immediately after the formation of these two island chars marked 'A' in the sketch map, those were at the disposal of the government. But it is the case of the defendant No. 2 and others that he, Kali Kanta Chatterjee, Anil Kumar Ghosh and Bhupendra Nath Das took lease of both the Chars in their totality from the government by executing four kabuliyats. The kabuliyat executed by Kali Kanta Chaterjee has not been produced in Court as because in spite of being called for the government who is supposed to be in custody of the same, did not file it. But the other three kabuliyats executed in the year 1946 have been filed in Court and marked as A, A(1) and A(2). These three documents prove that defendant Abdul Haque Sarker, Anil Kumar Ghosh and Bhupendra Nath Das executed kabuliyat in favour of the government for 4.79 acres of land each of the two island chars. Mr. Moazzem Hossain tried to argue that mere execution of the kabuliyats cannot create tenancy in favour of these executants unless the same were accepted by the government and the executants were recognised as tenants. But the documents Ext. A, A(I) and A(2) show that these were accepted by Khas Mohal Officer, Khulna and the said Officer also attested the same as witness. Moreover, these sets of defendants filed series of dakhilas to prove that they paid rent to the government for their leased land. So there cannot be any doubt about the fact that the two chars after becoming cultivable, were leased out by the government to defendant No. 1 Abdul Haque Sarder, Kali Kanta Chatterjee, Haran Kumar Ghosh and Bhupendra Nath Das in 1946 and subsequently rent was also accepted from them. With the leasing out of the land these four persons became tenure holders under the government and therefore on and from date of their acquisition of lease hold right over the two island chars clause (1) of section 4 of Regulation XI of 1825 became operative and by virtue of that provision of law they became entitled to anyadditional land which was gained to the two original island chars by recession of the river as increment to their tenure. Under the circumstances the plea taken by the government that since the two original chars marked 'A' in the Collector's sketch map, belonged to the government any accretion to them would automatically vest in the government is unacceptable. These accretions by operation of law as was in force at the time of such accretion, went to the tenure holders and their under tenants as well as the transferees as increment to their holdings. Of course, if the other set of defendants namely defendant Nos. 24-25, 26, 27, 30, 31-37 and 38-39 could show that these newly risen lands were reformation in situ of their land which previously were diluviated, then their claim would get preference. The documents filed in the trial Court show that by Ext. B one of the lease holders Kali Kanta Chatterjee, leased out his share to defendant No. 3, Sk. Nuruddin, that defendant No. 4, Emdad Ali Khan purchased the share for Buhpendra by kabala Ext. F and one Mahbubur Rahman purchased this interest of Anil Kumar by Ext. F(2) who in turn sold it to defendant Nos. 5-7 by Ext. F(1). These persons possessed their respective land in the islands and paid rent to the government and obtained dakhilas marked Ext. B series. The sketch map also shows that the accreted lands which are subject matter of the dispute depicted as blocks 1 to 5, surround the original northern island char of 2.55 acres while block Nos. 6 and 7 are contiguous to original southern island char of 16.60 acres and those have been attached by the Collector, being subject matter of contention between the parties and cause of apprehension of breach of peace. It may also be mentioned here that the kabuliyats marked Ext. A to A(2) contained the stipulation that in case of increase in the area of four lease hold lands the lessees would be liable to pay increased rent. This stipulation in other words means that the lessees would be entitled to any accretion that may happen to the areas of the original leased out land. In the Collector's map two khals or channels have been shown, one running between the block Nos. 2 and 3 and the other one between the block Nos. 6 and 7. PW 1, the District Kanungo tried to make out a case that these khals were navigable but he could not give the exact depth of the khals and on the other hand, he admitted that he had no personal knowledge of the origin of the khals or if they were fordable or not. On the other hand, DW 1 categorically stated that the khals were fordable at the time of formation of the disputed chars and that subsequently those have further silted up. Defendant Nos. 2-11, 12-18 and 21 and 23 claimed the disputed land as accretion to their tenancies. It. has been already stated that kabuliyats dated 18-10-46, 6-9-49 and 26.5.46 show that 4.79 acre of lands were taken settlement by each of DW 1 Abdul Haque Sarder, Kali Kanta Chatterjee and Anil 

 Kanta Ghosh at a rental of Rs. 3.00 per acre. It has also been shown that defendant Nos. 3-7 acquired the interest of Kali Kanta, Anil Ghosh and Bhupcn Das. Defendant No. 2 Abdul Haque Sarker claims 2.55 acres in the northern island and 2.23 acres in the southern island and also 28.00 acres as accretion to his original leased land. Out of these lands he has let out some to tenants who are parties in the suit and who support him. On the other hand, defendant Nos. 24-39 claim reformation in situ. Defendant Nos. 24-27 claim that disputed land originally were in mouza Jalma which was to the west of river Kazibacha while Tetultala was on the east, that during CS operation the river receded towards the north, south and was causing diluvion of some land of Jalma. Their further case is that the diluviated land subsequently re-appeared in their original sites, that Nanibala and others were tenure holders of mouza Jalma and on reformation these tenure holders brought Title Suit No. 5 of 1939 which was subsequently renumbered as 20/41 for the recovery of khas possession of these re-appeared land and obtained part decree in respect of the land described in schedule "kha" to the plaint of that suit and that their claim with respect to schedule "Ka" was dismissed. Their further case is that after obtaining decree these tenure holders settled the land with different tenants including defendant Nos. 24-27. So the sheet anchor of the claim of the these defendants is the decree obtained by their superior landlords in TS No. 20 of 1941. Admittedly the suit was with respect to the land of Jalma. But these defendants in the present suit did not take any attempt to relay the map attached to the decree passed in TS No. 20/41 in order to ascertain that the decretal land of that suit are identical with any portion of the present disputed land as shown in blocks No. 1-7 of the Collector's map. There is no dispute about the fact that in the CS map the whole of the river Kazibacha was included within mouza Tetultala while the eastern boundary line of both Jalma and Rangiamari was the western bank of the river. It is also not disputed that even after the change of course of the river there runs a channel in between the accreted land and the two villages Jalma and Rangiamari. Therefore, without relying the connected village maps it cannot be said that the disputed land are contiguous part of village Jalma and Rangiamari or that these char lands have re-appeared in the old sites which were originally depicted as part of Jalma or Rangiamari. Moreover, in Title Suit No. 20 of 1941 the government and some of the present claimants were not made parties and as such the decree passed in that suit is not binding upon them. Defendant No. 30 as DW 14 claims possession over the land. But from his deposition it transpires that he has no idea about the land and has no paper to show his possession. In that view of the matter, the trial Court has rightly held that the document Ext.A(9) is a spurious one. Defendant Nos. 31-37 claim 49.88 acres under the patta dated 13th Falgoon, 1354 BS marked Ext. A(7) purported to have been executed by Bhaigyadhar and Rajeshwar. The identity of this land has not been established by relaying the map. The Pleader Commissioner DW 18 said that he visited the land but in the next breath he said that plot No. 101 was under water at the time of his visit. On scrutiny of his deposition it appears that this Commissioner prepared his report Exts B(7) and C(7) sitting in his house without visiting the locality. Moreover, the map and the report in question were prepared by him in connection with Title Suit No. 155 of 1951 which suit is still pending and the report and the map of the Commissioner have not been accepted by the Court as yet. Kiran Biswas as DW 13 claimed that up to Kartick, 1355 BS Bhaigyadhar and defendant Nos. 31-37 possessed the land but could not produce any documentary evidence to substantiate his contention. He did not know if defendant Nos. 2, 3 and others took settlement of the land from government by executing four kabuliyats. Again, in a proceeding under section 145 CrPC this very witness claimed some land appertaining to mouza Tetultala. Thus he himself destroyed his credibility by saying one thing at one time and another at another time. Moreover, these defendants also did not take any step to get the land surveyed for the purpose of establishing their identity. Amrit Lal Guha who is said to have cultivated the land from 1362 BS has not been produced as witness. Moreover, DW 13 could not say who possessed plot Nos. 1009, 1015, 1045 and 1046 of block No. 2. From his cross-examination it transpires that the land of Rangiamari mouza is still under water and the entire land of block Nos. 1, 2 and 3 do not appeartain to that mouza. So he has virtually destroyed the case of this defendant that these three blocks reformed in the old situ and appertaining to Rangiamari mouza. Defendant Nos. 38 and 39 also did not give sufficient description of their land in their written statement. Defendant No. 

 27. Regulation XI of 1825 has not made any specific provision regarding the reformation in situ. Sub-section (5) of section 4 of the said Regulation provides that in case of claim which are not provided for by the rules laid down in section 4(1) to 4(4) the Courts shall be guided by a local usage, if there be any, and in the absence of such usage by the general principle of equity and justice. In the case of Lopez Vs. Mudun Tahakur, 13 MIA 467 the Privy Council laid down the principle that when an estate is gradually swallowed by the river or the sea and afterwards re-appeared on the old site and is capable of identification it is the property of the original owner and not an accretion to the estate to which it is attached unless there has been an abandonment by the original owner. Thus the cardinal principle is that in order to succeed on a claim of reformation in situ the identity of the land must be established by satisfactory evidence and that original owners cannot claim title if they after diluvion, had abandoned their rights by remission of revenue or by adverse possession. Keeping this principle in mind if we scrutinise the evidence on record as adduced by defendant Nos. 24-25, 26, 27, 30, 31-37 and 38-39 it become clear that they have miserably failed to establish their claim to the satisfaction of a reasonable mind. It has been stated earlier that they did not take any step to relay the disputed land so as to establish their identity with the alleged diluviated land. There is practically no credible evidence to prove that they resumed possession of these lands immediately on reformation without abandoning their claim. The plea of reformation in situ cannot be sustained unless it is proved that the land appearing as char is the same land which was lost by diluvion and that the claimants possessed the same land both before diluvion and after reformation. The above mentioned defendants miserably failed to prove these two points. It may be mentioned here that witness Nos. 11-14 could not even say accurately as to how and when defendant Nos. 24-27 and 30 to 39 possessed the disputed land or that these defendants paid rent before the diluvion and after reformation. A single dakhila Ext. A(5) of the year 1366 BS has been rightly termed as spurious by the trial Court. Defendant Nos. 40-51 whose claims have been dismissed by the trial Court have not come forward with any appeal. Similar is the case with defendant No.8. Under the circumstances the learned Subordinate Judge after discussing the evidence of DWs 2-6 and 9 who stated that no tenant of Rangiamari or Jalma ever possessed the disputed land since their appearance, has rightly come to the conclusion that defendant Nos. 43-55 abandoned their right, if any, by non-payment of rent and by not possessing the same for more than 12 years. 

 28. Considering the evidence on record both oral and documentary, we hold that the learned Subordinate Judge on proper sifting of the evidence on record has rightly come to the conclusion that defendant Nos. 2-7, 9, 12-18 and 21-22 have successfully proved their claim of title and possession over the disputed land, while defendant Nos. 8, 19, 24-27 and 30-51 could not prove their claim and defendant Nos. 20, 28 and 29 did not come forward to lay any claim over the disputed land at the time of trial. 

 29. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed lastly contended that in the decree the learned Subordinate Judge has not specifically ascertained the quantum of land which the successful defendants could get out of the accreted land and as such the decree suffers from vagueness. We are unable to agree with him. The Court has passed decree in favour of defendant Nos. 2-7, 9, 12-18 and 21-23 declaring their title and recovery of possession jointly. So these defendants can in future file a suit for partition amongst themselves and in that event the quantum of the accreted land to which each of them would be entitled will be ascertained by the Advocate Commissioner.

parties:
Abdus Samad @ AKM Abdus Samad and others ------- Petitioners.
Vs.
The State ------- Respondent.
full_judgment: 2. An incident of murder, rioting and criminal trespass took place on 20th November 1979 at about. 7'30 AM over the possession of a paddy land. Informant, PW 1, lodged an ejahar on which the police started this case and after investigation sent up these eleven petitioners for trial. Case of the prosecution is that the land belonged to, and was in possession of, his wife PW 2, that the informant with his labourers including one Giasuddin (the deceased) went to reap paddy of the land, but the petitioners formed an unlawful assembly, with the common object to kill the labourer and in prosecution of that common object, four of them caused the death of Giasuddin. The defence case is that the land was in possession of the petitioners, who claimed their title from the original c.s. recorded owners, Zuna Ram and Zeen Ram and that it was the informant's party, who had come to take forcible possession of the land and that in a free-fight that followed the labourer, Giasuddin, received fatal injuries from unknown assailants and that the petitioners simply exercised the right of private defence of their property.
case_type_name: Criminal Petition for Leave to Appeal

parties:
Sahera Khatun and another -------- Defendant-Appellant. 
 Vs. 
Anwara Khatun and others -------- Plaintiff-Respondents.
full_judgment:
A TM Afzal, J. : This appeal by defendants Nos. 2 and 3, following leave, arises out of judgment and order dated 16 August, 1990 passed by a Single Judge of the High Court Division, Dhaka in Civil Revision No. 837 of 1985 discharging the Rule and upholding the concurrent decree of the Courts below in Title Suit No.197 of 1977 . 

 2. Plaintiff-respondent No. 1 filed the aforesaid suit, originally numbered as Title Suit No. 68 of 1974 in the Third Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka and on transfer to the Fourth Court renumbered as above praying for a declaration that the decree dated 20.9.72 passed in Title Suit No. 35 of 1971 by the Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, in respect of the suit property is void and not binding on the plaintiff, that the kabala dated 23.2.73 obtained through court in Title Execution Case No. 32 of 1972 is null and void and that the sale deed dated 8.3.73 executed by defendant No. 1 (respondent No. 2) in favour of defendant No. 2 (appellant No. 1) is void and not binding on the plaintiff. 

 3. The case of the plaintiff, in substance, is that the suit property along with other properties originally belonged to 3(three) brothers, Nibaran Chandra Mitra, Abinash Chandra Mitra and Satish Chandra Mitra who acquired the same by purchase on 21.4.1914. The joint properties of three brothers were amicably partitioned and the suit property fell in the saham of Abinash Chandra Mitra who died leaving behind three sons, defendant Nos. 4-6 (respondents 3-5), the Mitras, who transferred the suit property to the plaintiff by a registered deed of exchange on 13.11.63 through their constituted Attorney Syed Amir Ali. The plaintiff has been in possession of the same on payment of all rents and taxes. The suit property was requisitioned by the erstwhile Province of East Pakistan and after transfer the name of the plaintiff was mutated and he was paid monthly compensation by the Government. But subsequently the Government stopped payment and as such the plaintiff had to me Title Suit No. 107 of 1973 against the Government. In the said suit defendant No. 2 of the instant suit impleaded herself as defendant No. 7 and filed a written statement claiming that defendants No. 4-6 entered into an agreement with defendant No. 1 to sell the suit property and defendant No. 1 obtained an ex parte decree for specific performance of contract in Title Suit No. 35 of 1971. The plaintiff alleged that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 35 of 1971 was obtained fraudulently by suppressing all processes etc. Defendant Nos. 4-6 left the country long ago and had been residing in India permanently and they did not enter into any agreement with defendant No.1. Defendant No. 1 created the deed of agreement by practising fraud and obtained the ex parte decree by the same means. Hence the decree dated 20.9.72 obtained by defendant No. 1 in the said suit was null and void and the subsequent kabala in execution of the said decree did not confer any title to defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 2 did not acquire any title by her alleged purchase from defendant No. 1. The said decree and the subsequent deeds cast a cloud on the title of the plaintiff and as such the plaintiff had to file the suit. 

 5. Defendant Nos. 8 and 9, the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property and the Government also filed a written statement contending that the suit property was requisitioned in 1948 and the name of the plaintiff was mutated as owner in place of the Mitras, that defendant No. 3 was an allottee, that the suit property has since been derequisitioned and that the decree obtained by defendant No. 1 in Title Suit No. 35 of 1971 is null and void. 

 6. The suit was once decreed earlier. The defendant-appellants went in appeal, title Appeal No.103 of 1978, which was dismissed and then they took a revision, Civil Revision No.1065 of 1979, in which the Rule was made absolute by the High Court Division and an order of remand to the trial court was passed. The remand was felt necessary because the High Court Division observed that the question of title of the plaintiff was directly and substantially in issue in the suit and without deciding that issue the plaintiff could not be given any relief under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and that a decision on the issue of title would also decide her locus standi to file the suit. After remand the plaintiff amended her plaint and at the trial, besides five issues already framed, three additional issues were taken up for consideration which are as follows: 

 7.	 Has the plaintiff claimed title to the suit property? 

 9.	 Is the ex parte decree in TS 35n 1 of the 3rd Court of Sub-Judge, Dhaka a fraudulent, void and did the consequent sale deed in favour of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 confer any title to the said defendants? 

 7.	The learned Subordinate Judge 4th Court, Dhaka by his judgment dated 28 April, 1983 decreed the suit again upon deciding all the issues in favour of the plaintiff. The title of the plaintiff was clearly found and as to issue No. 8 above it was found that the impugned ex parte decree and the Kabalas in pursuance of the same were obtained by practising fraud upon the court and as such defendant Nos. 1 and 2 did not acquire any title on the basis of the said documents. 

 8.	The appellants took an appeal against the said decree, Title Appeal No. 145 of 1983, which was dismissed by the Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka by his judgment dated 10 November 1985. Thereafter they filed a revision, Civil Revision No. 837 of 1985, in which the impugned judgment and order were passed. 

 9.	One of the main contentions of the contesting defendants in the suit was that the plaintiff had not acquired any title to the suit property on the basis of the deed of Exchange dated 13.11.63 (Ext. 2) because she had no right, title, interest or possession over any portion of the alleged property of Murshidabad, West Bengal the ownership of which was alleged to have been transferred to the exchangees, i.e. the Mitras as mentioned in Ext.2 Since the plaintiff was not the owner of the Murshidabad property, there was no transfer of ownership in exchange and as such the document Ext. 2 was void. At the hearing of the suit defendant No.3 (husband of defendant No. 2) who examined himself as DW 1 proved certain documents procured from and certified by Notary Public in India which were admitted into evidence without any objection. The Additional District Judge, inter alia, observed that the said documents were not admissible as those were not authenticated by the Bangladesh Mission in India. During pendency of the revisional application the said documents were got authenticated and an application was filed under Order 41 rule 27 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for accepting the documents in deciding the revision case. 

 11.	The High Court Division upon making reference to Sec. 119 of the Transfer of Property Act which provides for the right of a party deprived of thing received in exchange observed that even if the plaintiff failed to prove her title to the Murshidabad property the deed of exchange cannot be said to be invalid and that it is not necessary to decide whether the plaintiff had title to those properties. Being of such view the High Court Division did not think it necessary to consider the aforesaid documents. 

 13. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the appellants, referred to the definition of 'Exchange' in section 118 of the TP Act and submitted that in a valid exchange there must be a mutual transfer of ownership of the properties between the parties to the exchange and since in the present case the documents as referred to above prove that the plaintiff had no title to and ownership over the properties of Murshidabad which were allegedly given to the Mitras by her in exchange, there was no exchange in the eye of law and the deed of exchange Ext. 2 was void. The suit being one for declaration of title of the plaintiff she was bound to prove that there was a valid exchange. Mr. Ahmed submitted that the view taken by the High Court Division was not in keeping either with the law or with the requirement of the suit. Mr. Ahmed also submitted that the High Court Division erred in totally ignoring the aforesaid documents of the defendant-appellants which has caused a miscarriage of justice. 

 14. Mr. Nurul Huq, learned Advocate-on-Record for the plaintiff-respondent, submitted that the contesting defendants being strangers to the exchange, they had no locus standi to question the validity of the exchange when the exchangees, the Mitras, who were made parties to the suit did not come to deny the transaction. It was a sufficient proof that there was a valid exchange and no further proof of the plaintiffs title to the Indian property was necessary. 

 15. Mr. Huq submitted that in the facts and circumstances of the case the view taken by the High Court Division was fully justified and no error was committed by the learned judge in not considering the Khatians etc. produced by the defendants which the plaintiff had alleged to be wrong and forged. Nevertheless, the lower Appellate Court fully considered the said document and rejected them, he pointed out. The two courts below having concurrently found title of the plaintiff and it having been further found that the defendants' decree and subsequent kabalas were vitiated by fraud, the High Court Division committed no error in discharging the Rule upon the view taken, Mr. Huq finally submitted. 

 16. Section 118 of the TP Act defines "Exchange". It says when two persons mutually transfer the ownership of one thing for the ownership of another, neither thing or both things being money only, the transaction is called an "Exchange". An exchange is a mutual transfer between two persons of the ownership of properties, but either both the things should be money or neither of them should be money. Therefore, transfer of ownership is a pre-condition for a valid exchange. When there is a question of title to be decided on the basis of an exchange deed, the party claiming title must prove that he had ownership in the property exchanged which had been transferred under the exchange. How it will be proved or when it is said to have been proved different matter. A party to the exchange when deprived of the thing or any part of the thing received by him in exchange because of any defect in the title of the other party has his remedy under section 119. But that is not to say that a third party can never raise the question of title of a party to the exchange. For example, in the present case, the defendants claiming title to themselves of the disputed property were competent to question the plaintiffs exchange. Therefore, the learned Judge of the High Court Division was not quite right in observing that even if the plaintiff failed to prove her title to the Murshidabad property the exchange cannot be said to be invalid or that it is not necessary to decide whether the plaintiff had title to those properties. Notwithstanding the said observations, however, the learned Judge was particular to notice that the lower appellate Court observed that the Mitras were satisfied with the title and possession of the plaintiff in the Murshidabad property as asserted by PWs 1 and 2 and there was no evidence from the side of the defendants to controvert the aforesaid evidence of PW s 1 and 2 and that the Mitras though made parties to the suit not one of them raised any objection or contested the suit. 

 17. The learned Judge satisfied himself that the Court of fact has found that the plaintiffs' title to and ownership over the Indian property was proved satisfactorily. 

 19. The learned Additional District Judge besides considering the defendants evidence as to alleged lack of title of the plaintiff went on to say that PWs 1 and 2 clearly stated that the plaintiffs title deeds were handed over to the Mitras, that PW 2 clearly stated that the Mitras were satisfied with the title and possession of the plaintiff, that the Mitras did not raise any objection or contest the suit, that the Government also did not raise any objection with regard to the title of the plaintiff as to her Murshidabad property, that the exchanges of the respective properties were made by both the parties in compliance with section 118 of the TP Act, that the certified copy of the Mitras' exchange deed was referred to in Ext. 2 and submitted to the Registrar's office and that as such it is futile to say that the plaintiff had no properties at Murshidabad, After such findings, the High Court Division had very little to do in revision when the said findings could not be assailed legally. It was not essential for the High Court Division to review the defendants' aforesaid documents over again because the Additional District Judge gave good reasons for not relying upon them. We have, however, ourselves perused the documents at the instance of the appellants. The Khatians which have been produced are of a date which is fourteen years after the execution of the exchange deed. The information slips by themselves do not carry much probative value. The plaintiff denied the said documents alleging them to be false and forged. Considering the evidence and circumstances in their totality, the court of fact (Additional District Judge) found that it was futile to say that the plaintiff had no properties at Murshidabad. There is no good reason to think that the said finding was for any reason erroneous or untenable. Therefore, it cannot be said that the learned Judge of the High Court Division misdirected himself to an extent causing an error in the decision and/or resulting in a failure of justice.

parties:
Farida Aziz ----- Petitioner.
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works and Urban Development, Secretariat Building, Dhaka and anr. ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Mr. PBA Selim was the original owner of the house namely Holding No. 300 (old), Road No. 25 Dhanmondi Residential Area, Dhaka which he constructed after obtaining lease of a plot of land from the Government under a registered deed of lease dated 26.6.57. Mr. Selim while serving in the United Nations Economic Commission for Asia and Far East in Bangkok, Thailand met with an accident and died on August 25,1964. He left behind as his only heirs a minor son, Irshad Selim and a minor daughter Akter Selim. His wife predeceased him Mr. Selim bequeathed the aforesaid building property to his son and daughter Irshed Selim and Akhter Selim and appointed his brother-in-law Mr. KM Nasiruddin the Executor of the will. Mr. Nasiruddin duly obtained probate on July 6,1973 from the Court of District Judge, Dhaka and the aforesaid children of late Mr. Selim became owners in moiety share on the strength of the will and were in possession. Mr. Nasiruddin as a guardian of minor children leased out the building to the Bangladesh Cha Sanshad from before liberation of Bangladesh and the said tenant continued in possession till June 1973, Subsequently, by and under an agreement of lease executed in June, 1973 between Mr. KA Dewan, a member of National Board of Revenue (NBR) and Mr. Nasiruddin the house was leased out to Mr. KA Dewan who continued in possession till September, 1977 when the Government took over possession from Mr. KA Dewan and since then it is being treated as abandoned property by the Government. The owners of the house thereafter made several applications (Annexure E to E-5) to different authorities including the Ministry of Works for excluding the house from the list of the abandoned property and to release the same in their favour. As a result of controversy as to whether the property is an abandoned or not the Joint Secretary to the Ministry of Works and Urban Development by an order dated October, 2, 1975 (Annexure E-6 to this petition) stated that the house in question cannot be treated as an abandoned property and as Nasiruddin was a pension holder and never parted with the administration and supervision of his property a direction to maintain status quo in regard to the building was given. Nasiruddin entered into an agreement for sale of the aforesaid property with the petitioner for legal necessity and for better provision of the minor children of late Selim for consideration of Tk. 1,50,000.00 and on receipt of Tk. 1,05,000.00 he executed the said agreement on June 29,1973 but could not execute the deed of sale as formalities to execute and register the deed could not be completed. In the meanwhile on attaining their majority Arshad Selim and Akhtar Selim entered into a fresh agreement for sale of the house with the petitioner on October 27, 1980. But later on their refusal to transfer the house the petitioner instituted the Title Suit No. 369 of 1983 for specific performance of contract in the court of Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka against Irshad Selim and Akhtar Selim impleading the Secretary, Ministry of Works and the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka as defendant Nos. 4 and 5 in the said suit. On several dates although defendant Nos. 4 and 5 took adjournments for filing written statement but it was not filed and the court ultimately on September 13,1985 decreed the suit ex-parte. Pursuant to the said decree the petitioner got the deed registered through court in respect of the house on July 7, 1986 and became the absolute owner of the house. 

 4. The Government respondent contested the case before the Court of Settlement without filing any written statement. The stand of the Government was that the petitioner and her vendors violated the term Nos. 19 to 27 of the original lease Agreement made between the Government of East Pakistan and Mr. PBA Selim and the property was being treated as abandoned property the respondent issued several notices upon the occupants of the house to produce documents, etc. to establish title of the original lessee and as the whereabouts of the alleged owners were not traceable the possession of the building was taken as an abandoned building which is in possession of Mr. ATM Shamsul Huq. 

 6. Mr. TH Khan first, submits that the Court of Settlement acted in excess of its jurisdiction in holding that as Nasiruddin and Mr. KA Dewan were served with notices to produce the title documents of the alleged successors of the property whose whereabouts were not known the Government rightly took possession of the house and legally included the same in schedule "Ka" of the list of the abandoned property published under section 5 of the aforesaid Ordinance and such inclusion conclusively established that the property was an abandoned property under PO 16 of 1972. The learned advocate continues to argue that without giving due consideration to the decree of the civil Court which was not set aside by a superior court at the instance of the Government or any other person having interest therein, the Court of Settlement committed serious illegality in so holding. Mr. Khan next contends that the Court of Settlement failed to decide the right of a citizen judicially without applying its mind to the relevant documents produced before it to prove that the property does not satisfy the description of abandoned property within the meaning of PO 16 of 1972. He further urges that the Court of Settlement in absence of any material to show that the Government formed its opinion that building is an abandoned property, the decision of the Court of Settlement suffers from excess of jurisdiction, He also contends that enlistment of abandoned property in question under schedule "KA" of the list was without any lawful authority inasmuch as the possession was taken by the Government from the legal tenant Mr. KA Dewan of the vendors of the petitioner. The respondent No. 1 contested this Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition. The learned Assistant Attorney-General, on the other hand, submits that as the whereabouts of Mr. Selim the original owner and his son Irshad Selim, and daughter Akhtar Selim were not known the Government treated the house as abandoned house and as such inclusion of the said house in the list of abandoned property was legally done and publication of the list in the official Gazette on September 23, 1986 was valid in law and the decisions of the Court of Settlement does not suffer from any defect of jurisdiction. 

 7. Before inclusion of the building in the list to be published under section 5 of the Ordinance 54 of 1985 as an abandoned property the conditions specified under section 5 must be satisfied. The conditions are that the owner must be found not to occupy, manage and supervise the building in person on the date of coming into force of PO 16 of 1972 and the whereabouts of the owner were not known and the Government has taken possession of the same. Neither in the Court of Settlement below nor before us anything except taking of possession in July, 1977 for the legal tenant of the vendors of the petitioner by the Respondent No. 1 could be placed to establish that the requirement of section 5 of the Ordinance were fulfilled. From a careful reading of Article 2 of PO 16 of 1972 it appears to us that in order to treat a property as an abandoned property the property must fall within the ambit of definition of abandoned property. One of the conditions as defined in Article 2 is that on the date of promulgation of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 the owner of the property must not occupy, manage or supervise the property and on fulfillment of such condition the property vests in the Government as an abandoned property and the Government is entitled to take possession thereof. In this case admittedly the Government took possession for the tenant of the owner. Whenever possession of a house is taken by the Government from a lawful tenant of the owner of the house taking of such possession is illegal for the purpose of treating the same as an abandoned property as the owner of the property is in the possession thereof through the tenant and the Government is not empowered to take possession of the house from the tenant treating the same as abandoned on the plea of absence of the owner temporarily from the house. Therefore the present building property does not fall within the meaning of "abandoned property" as defined in Article 2 of the Order. The decision cited by Mr. Khan in the case of MIs. Gonnysons Ltd. and another Vs. Sonali Bank and others, 37 DLR (AD) 42 supports this view. Mr. Khan also rightly relied on the decision in the case of Government of Bangladesh Vs. Mirza Shahab Ispanahi, 40 DLR (AD) 177. Inclusion of the house in question in the list of the abandoned property after taking possession from the tenant of Irshed Selim and Akhter Selim and publication of the same in the Gazette notification by the Government are not only without any sanction of law but also is the result of arbitrary action on the part of the Government in dealing with the property of a citizen. Such an action on the part of the respondent No. 1 is deprecated whose sole duty is to protect the life and property of the citizen of a democratic polity. Therefore, in our opinion, the Court of Settlement failed to exercise its jurisdiction in not passing an order for exclusion of the building property from the list of the abandoned property published in the Gazette notification on 23rd September, 1986. We are also of the opinion that the Court of Settlement did not at all apply its judicial mind to the material on record in making the impugned order as it is evident from the record that the respondent No. 1 took possession of the building from the lawful occupation of the tenant of the petitioner vendors. Being confronted with legal and factual position Mr. Delwar Hossain, the learned Assistant Attorney-General assisted by Mrs. Hosne Ara Ahsan, felt difficulty to support the judgment and order of the Court of Settlement and the inclusion of the building in the list in question.

parties:
Ahmed Hossain ----- Petitioner
vs
Dr AA Rizvi and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule obtained under section 115 (old) of the of Civil Procedure is directed against the order dated 15-2-77 passed by the learned Munsif, 6th Court, Dacca in Title Suit No. 52 of 1981 allowing an application by opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 for adding them as parties to the suit. 

 2. The petitioner as plaintiff instituted the said title suit for a declaration that the order by the defendants declaring the suit property as abandoned property is without jurisdiction, null and void etc. and for an order of permanent injunction restraining the defendants from allotting the suit property to anybody. The plaintiff petitioner claimed full ownership of the property in an auction sale in 1945. He asserted that he inducted one Mr. Rizvi a non-Bengali as his monthly tenant since 1945. He also stated that Mr Rizvi shifted elsewhere keeping the suit property under lock and key during the liberation war in 1971. 

 5. In their application under Order III, Rule, 10 CPC the defendant-opposite-parties stated that the suit property never belonged to the plaintiff petitioner. It belonged to one Mr. Sadaqat Hossain Dara who inducted the opposite parties as tenant in 1956. The suit property was sealed by the Deputy Commissioner, Dacca treating the business concern of the said opposite parties therein as abandoned. The said opposite parties filed an application under Article 15 of PO 16 of 1972 for release of their business concern in their favour. In the mean-while the plaintiff-petitioner occupied the suit property by unlocking the same and then filed the present title suit. The learned Munsif found that the added defendant-opposite-parties filed a number of rent receipts to show that they used to pay rent to one SH Dara. The petitioner could not file any counterfoil of any rent-receipt to show that he realised rent from the added defendant-opposite-parties. 

 7. Mr Abu Sayeed. Ahmed next submits that the ex-parte decree having been passed on 28-8-75 and ex-parte decree having not been set-aside the application of the added defendant opposite parties is not maintainable and the learned Munsif acted illegally and with material irregularity in not holding so. It appears that on 10-1-76 the original defendants in the title suit filed an application under Order IX, rule 13 CPC for restoration of the original suit and it further appears that the said application giving rise to Miscellaneous Case No. 6, of 1976 is still pending. It also appears that after the added defendant-opposite parties' application under Order 1, Rule 10 CPC was allowed by the learned Munsif on 15-2-77 they filed an application under Order IX, Rule 13 and section 151 CPC, for restoration of the Original suit. 

 8. It has been held in the case of Rameshwar Bhagat vs Thakur Jeban Barayan Singh AIR 1947 Patna, 49" where t the suit was decreed ex-parte and persons entitled to be added as parties to the suit make an application to add them as parties and to set-aside the ex-parte decree, Court should add them as parties and give them an opportunity to set-aside the ex-parte decree".

parties:
New India Tea Company Ltd. ----- Appellant.
Vs. 
Bangladesh and others ----- Respondent.
full_judgment:
5. Before the High Court the appellant-company contended that since the Union Agency Ltd., is a part and parcel of the appellant company, the title of the land in dispute belonged to it. On the other hand the Government's contention was that since the land belonged to the Union Agency Ltd. which has become an enemy concern, the Government was entitled to take it over as enemy property. The rule came up for final hearing before a Division Bench of the High Court which discharged the rule on May 25, 1977. 

 6. Mr. S.R. Pal, Counsel for the appellant, submitted that the earned Judges of the High Court were wrong in deciding the disputed question of facts relating to title to the land which could only have been done by taking proper evidence, oral and documentary Whether the relinquishment by Hirala Mukherjee, Manager of Ramgarh Tea Estate in whose favour the land was originally settled regally transferred title in favour of the Union Agency Ltd. depended on the decision as to whether a registered document was necessary to effect the relinquishment. The learned Counsel also submitted that the decision as to whether the Union Agency Ltd. was a part and parcel of the appellant-company required investigation into facts. It appears that the High Court did not believe the genuineness of the rent receipt dated 25.3.67 produced by the appellant-company in support of its claim that rent was being paid by the company to the Government and it also found discrepancies with respect to the Khatian number mentioned in the rent receipt. The land in dispute was recorded as Khatian No. 1/36 after the mutation case No. 2/1, whereas the rent receipt showed that rent was being paid in respect of land in Khatian No. 1/38. Further, there was no reason as to why the appellant-company whose name was not recorded in the Khatian should pay rent in respect of the land of which M/c. Union Agency Ltd. was the recorded tenant, The questions raised by the learned Counsel relate to the title of the appellant-company which depend on facts which are in dispute and can only be settled after full evidence has been properly taken. Mr. Sultan Hossain the learned Deputy Attorney General who appeared on be If of the Government also conceded that where facts are disputed; the high Court, in exercising jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution not proceed to settle the disputed facts requiring taking of evidence. There is a long line of decisions in favour of the view that the High Court should not enter in to disputed questions of fact nor decide any question as to title which require investigation into facts and taking of elaborate evidence.
