The land measuring 9.28 acres of CS plot Nos. 142, 143, 144, 145, 146, 147, 148 & 149 in CS Khatian No. 93 originally belonged to one Fadu Sajwal in 5 annas 2 karas 2 kerantis share, Ram Charan Sajwal, Adhar Chand Sajwal along with Jagabandhu Barik each in 2 annas 13 gandas 1 kara 1 keranti sahres and Rajani Barik, Jamini Barik, Bhadra Chandra Barik and Dukhi Barik each in 13 gandas 1 kara 1 keranti shares. The CS recorded tenant Gopal Sajwal died in his tender age living behind 2 full brothers Avoy Sajwal and Kanu Sajwal. The two brothers died unmarried and their property devolved upon their cousin Kukuri Sajwal. On the death of Kukuri Sajwal his only son Bhadra Kanta Sajwal became the sole owner. Subsequently Bhadra Kanta Sajwal died living behind only son Chandra Kanta Sajwal and on his death the plaintiff Nos. 1-3 remains his heirs. 

 In the RS operation 0.03 acres of land of CS plot No. 272 recorded in hal plot No. 1358 of RS Khatian No. 71. The plaintiff Nos.1-3 acquired 1.89 acre of land in equal shares which has been recorded in hal plot Nos. 1364 and 894 in 54 decimals and 1.35 acres of land respectively. The CS recorded tenants Harachandra and Durga Charan died living behind their sons Rashik Chandra and Prohalad Chandra. The CS recorded tenant Sree Charan Sawjal being unmarried died and his share devolved upon his two nephews namely Rashik Chandra and Prohalad Chandra in equal shares. On the death of Rashik Chandra his only son Upendra Sawjal inherited the property and after the death of Upendra Sawjal his son the plaintiff No. 9 Uttam Kumar Sawjal inherited the property left behind him. On the death of Prohalad Sawjal his son plaintiff No. 10 Ananta Kumar Sawjal inherited the property and in this way the plaintiff Nos. 9 and 10 each acquired 0.79½ acres of land in equal shares. The further case of the plaintiffs is such that the recorded owner of CS Khatian No. 35 Proshanna Kumar Sawjal died living behind only son the plaintiff No. 5 Jogendra Nath Sawjal and on the death of Brindaban Sawjal his only son Rajani Sawjal became the heir. On the death of Rajani Sawjal his son Mukunda Nath inherited the land of Rajani and on the death of Mukunda Nath plaintiff No. 4 Lakshmi Kanta as his only son inherited. During RS operation 2.13 acres of land in CS plot No. 274 under CS Khatian No. 35 has been recorded in hal plot No. 894 which is also the suit land. During RS operation although some part of 9.42 acres of land in CS plot Nos.173-180 under CS Khatian No. 66 was recorded in the names of the predecessors of the plaintiffs along with some others in RS Khatian Nos.17/18 corresponding to SA Khatian Nos. 24 and 25 in hal plot Nos. 170, 171, 168, 169, 187, 148, 166, 167, 149, 150, 151, 152, 153 and 154, but 0.09 acres of land out of 0.20 acres from plot No. 176, the entire 1.67 acres of CS plot No. 177, 0.03 acres out of 0.59 acres of CS plot No. 178, 0.10 acres out of 0.81 acres of land in CS plot No. 179 and 0.84 acres out of 1.69 acres of CS Plot No. 180 in all 2.73 acres of land recorded in hal plot No. 894. The CS recorded tenant Dasharath died unmarried living behind only brother Haricharan Sawjal, who died unmarried living behind his nephew Chandra Kanta Sajwal. On the death of CS recorded tenant Goalak Bashi and Mohon Bashi their total shares devolved upon their nephews in absence of their sons and daughters in equal share. The aforesaid nephews are one Rajani Kanta and Jogendra Nath, who is the plaintiff No. 5 of the suit. During RS operation though some part of 9.28 acres of land of CS plot Nos.143-149 under CS Khatian No. 93 recorded in the names of the predecessors of the plaintiffs along with some others in RS Khatian No. 37 corresponding to SA Khatian No. 48 in hal plot Nos. 140-147, but the entire 0.83 acres of land of CS Plot No. 143 the area measuring 2.48 acres of CS plot No. 144, 0.27 acres of CS plot No. 145, 0.32 acres out of 0.86 acres of land in CS plot No. 146, 0.71 acres out of 1.00 acre in CS Plot No. 147 in all 4.61 acres of land recorded in hal plot No. 894, which is part of the disputed land. Plaintiff's further case is such that the owner of the 1/3rd share of CS Khatian No. 93 Fasu Sawjal died as widow without any issue living behind only nephew Bhadra Kanta. On the unmarried death of Adhar Chand 2 annas 13 ganda 1 kara 1 kranti share devolved upon his nephew Ram Doyal. Ram Doyal being the owner of 5 annas 6 gandas 2 karas 2 kerantis share died living behind 2 sons Sumon and Dhiran. On the death of Sumon Sawjal his share devolved upon his only son the plaintiff No. 6 Krishna Kanta and on the death of Dhiran his share devolved upon his 2 sons the plaintiff Nos. 7 and 8. After the death of Rajani, Jamini, Bhadra Kanta and Dukhi Chandra Barik their entire share devolved upon their nephew Bhadra Kanta Sawjal and after the death of Bhadra Kanta his 3 sons the plaintiff Nos. 1-3 inherited the property. In this way out of the entire suit land measuring an area of 12.95 acres of land, the plaintiff Nos. 1-3 acquired 2.73½ acres of land each. The plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5 acquired 0.80 3/4 acres of land each, plaintiff No. 6 acquired 0.76 3/4 acres of land, plaintiff Nos. 7 and 8 acquired 0.38¼ acres of land and plaintiff Nos. 9 &10 each acquired 0.79½ acres of land and they have been enjoying the same peacefully and uninterruptedly since the day of reappearance of the land by way of cultivation. In the RS operation, the said land, recorded in hal plot Nos.1364 and 894 as 0.54 acres and 12.41 acres respectively. It is the positive case of the plaintiffs that the suit property went under water of the river Arial Kha in the year 1339 BS and its diluvion was completed in the year 1445 BS. Subsequently the land re-appeared again in the other side of the river within 10 years. As the RS operation of the corresponding area was started in the year 1346 BS corresponding to 1939 AD and finally published in 1358-1359 BS, in the remark column, the suit property was wrongly shown as river and used by the public at large. Subsequently SA record was also prepared in the aforesaid manner as it was a table work relying upon the RS Khatians. The suit property was wrongly shown under water of the river Arial Kha, despite the same has already been reappeared long before. Being inspired by the said wrong record the Tahashilder of the defendant government of Bangladesh on 15-11-2005 claimed the suit disowning the right, title and interest of the plaintiffs. Hence the plaintiffs filed the original suit for declaration of title. 

 3. The contrary case of the defendant in short is thus, that the suit property went under water of the river Arial Kha in the year 1939 BS and it remained under water for a period of 70/75 years. As such due to the sikasti (diluvion) character of the property a note in the remark column of the corresponding and RS and SA Khatian was given showing the suit property in the river and being used by public at large, which is correct. The suit property started to reappear just before 3/4 years and the defendant government is under process of its allotment. The further case of the defendant-appellant-opposite party is such that the suit property remained under water of the river Arial Kha for a period of 70/75 years and as a result the plaintiffs have no right, title, interest and possession therein. After reappearance of the land in hal plot No. 1364, the defendant allotted the same in favour of third party vide Miscellaneous Case No. 1862/60-61 and some new Khatians has also been opened in the names of those allottees. The land of hal plot No. 894 also allotted to different persons and the suit property is yet to be fit for cultivation and the same is still a lower shore of the river Arial Kha and in near future as the suit property would become fit for cultivation, the plaintiffs filed the suit for illegal gain. 

 4. The Trial Court, i.e. learned Assistant Judge, Muladi, Barisal in Title Suit No. 106 of 2005 after framing four issues as to the maintainability of suit, right, title and interest of the plaintiffs and entitlement of the plaintiffs to have the suit be decreed examining three witnesses for the plaintiffs and one witness for the defendants decreed the suit on contest. 

 5. Being aggrieved the defendant prefer-red an appeal being Title Appeal No. 114 of 2009 in the Court of the learned District Judge, Barisal, which was heard and disposed of by the learned Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Barisal and the learned Appellant Court below by the impugned judgment and decree dated 3-11-2010 allowed the appeal reversing the judgment and decree passed by the learned Trial Court. 

 8. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that the learned Appellate Court below during disposal of the appeal committed gross illegality and irregularity in deciding the merit of the appeal. The learned Advocates further submits that during disposal of the appeal there has been glaring misreading and non-reading of the evidence and non-consideration of the material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocates also submits that the findings on possession of the Trial Court not at all reversed by the Appellate Court below and the possession inasmuch as, in favour of the plaintiffs as observed by the Trial Court is unrebutted, the impugned judgment is not sustainable in law. The learned Counsels further submit that the possession follows the title and non payment of rent does not extinguish title of the plaintiffs in the suit property. Without reversing the findings and decisions of the Trial Court the decision of the Appellant Court below as transpires is not in accordance with law and in this context the learned Advocates referred a decision of our Apex Court reported in 16 MLR (AD) 4 in the case of Abdur Rashid vs Afzal Gazi The learned Advocate lastly submits that the defendant to the suit during examination of the plaintiff's witness as because not cross-examined the witness specially the PW No.1 (plaintiff No. 1) upon the year of diluvion and alluvion of the suit land, the observation and findings of the lower Appellate Court have no leg to stand as per section 137 of the Evidence Act and, as such, the specific contention on the fact of alluvion and diluvion of the land as stated from the side of the plaintiffs has become admitted by the act of the adversary. In this connection another decision has been referred from the side of the petitioners decided in the case of Mst. Zarjan vs Mst. Nazmunnessa reported in 1969 PLD 118. The learned Trial Court after thorough assessment of evidence and appreciation of law and on careful consideration of the facts, circumstances and papers on record decreed the suit, but the lower Appellant Court without reversing the findings of the Trial Court in consultation with the evidence on record reversed the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Muladi, Barisal illegally and that the Appellate Court below committed an error of law in not considering that the revisional survey in the field conducted in between the years 1933-1942 while the land was on the verse of reformation and the RS Khatian was published in the year 1952 within which the land has been completely reformed. The learned Joint District Judge also erred in law having failed to consider that the disputed land has reformed in situ within statutory period and, as such, before the promulgation of part V of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, the land in dispute was reformed as a whole and become fit for cultivation. 

 13. On perusal of the original case records along with the Exhibited papers including the deposition of the witnesses it transpires that the plaintiffs in support their respective case produced the relevant CS Khatians, RS Khatians, SA Khatians, plot index and the certified copies of the approved Sketch Map (Kalami Naksha) of the government and those papers were duly marked Exhibits. The pertinent question in the instant suit is, as to when the suit property reappeared from the garb of the river Arial Kha. The Trial Court relied upon the testimonies of the witnesses and the witnesses specially the witness no. 2 Arun Mandal and 3 Santosh, who are the inhabitants of the concerned area Saheber Chor. These two competent, credible witnesses specifically asserted that from their boyhood they are finding the suit property under cultivation of the plaintiffs and the plaintiffs are enjoying the same uninterrupted. The defendant government alleged that in Miscellaneous Case No. 1862 of 60-61 some allottees obtained allotment of the suit property from the government as 'Khas' land and the allottees since their allotment are in possession over the same. But it appears from the case record that no authentic paper or any competent credible oral evidence is coming from the side of the government supporting the same. The positive case of the plaintiffs is such that the property in dispute reappeared within ten years from the date of diluvion which is long before part-V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The diluvion process starts in the year of 1339 BS and continued up to 1345 BS and within 10 years from 1345 BS the land reappeared which is the positive case of the plaintiffs while the defendant's plea that the property remained under water for 70/75 years and it has started to re appear only 3-4 years before filing of the original suit is not supported by any documentary or oral evidence. The learned Trial Court positively held that the testimonies of the plaintiff's witnesses makes it clear that the land in dispute in fact reappeared from the bed of the river Arial Kha within ten years from the diluvion process which was continued up to 1345 BS vis-a-vis; we have came across from the solitary oral evidence from the side of the defendant opposite-party that the witness Md. Serajul Islam states in the deposition that the land went under water in the year 1339 BS and some portion of the land subsequently reappeared and settlement process is going on for the said portion, which has be-come fit for cultivation. This witness Serajul Islam is an official of Upazila land office, Muladi. He is a formal witness and as surveyor he joined in the office on 15-9-2005 AD. He admits that, supporting the case of the government no paper submitted save and except the written statement. On the contrary the witness No. 1 of the plaintiffs is Samir Chandra Sawjal, who is the plaintiff No. 1 of the suit. He corroborated their plaint case as a whole to the genealogy along with their acquisition of the property by way of inheritance from their predecessors in interest. It is not denied from the side of the defendant-opposite party that the predecessors of the plaintiffs were the original owners of the property and that the CS record in their names is correct. The plaintiff No. 1 in his testimony categorically states at a stage that the land in dispute went under water within the years 1339-1345 BS and thereafter within ten years it reappears. Finally in the year 1355 BS the land has become fit for cultivation. The other witnesses of the plaintiffs i.e. the witnesses No. 2 and 3, who are the possession witnesses corroborated the plaintiffs in respect of their possession in the disputed property. 

 14. On perusal of the impugned judgment and decree of the lower Appellate Court it appears that the learned Joint District Judge during disposal of the appeal utterly failed to consider the point of controversy between the parties as well as the criterion of the suit. There is no dispute regarding the time of diluvion of the suit property in the bed of the river Arial Kha. As regard alluvion of the property i.e. reappearance of the same the dispute runs and in this context it is noticed that the contention advanced from the side of the plaintiffs is acceptable since it is proved by sufficient competent, credible, tangible evidence. The leaned Trial Court during disposal of the original suit in his findings and observation most emphatically pointed out that when and between how may years the land in dispute reappeared from the bed of the river Arial Kha. But the learned Appellate Court below without reversing the positive findings of the trial Court in a hasty evasive manner decided that the plaintiff's claim is not proved, while the defendant government has made out their case in respect of the property claimed. Not only this; the leaned Appellate Court during disposal of the appeal was misconceived and relied upon illegally on the testimony of the defendant's witness, who is not at all a competent credible witness and measurably failed to establish the bonafide of the defendant. 

 22. In the result, the Rule having merit is made absolute. The impugned judgment and decree dated 3-11-2010 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Barisal in Title Appeal No. 114 of 2009 allowing the appeal and setting-aside those dated 19-4-2009 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Muladi, Barisal in Title Suit No. 106 of 2005 is hereby set-aside.

parties:
Government of Bangladesh and others …… Appellants (In all the appeals) 
Vs
Abdul Motaleb & others……. Respondents (In all the appeals)
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J: These appeals, by Leave, by the plaintiff arise out of the judgment and order dated 23-7-2002 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision Nos. 3863, 4612 and 4613 of 1998 making all the Rules absolute by setting aside the judgment and decree dated 4-6-1998 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Patuakhali in Title Appeal Nos. 5, 87 and 116 of 1992 reversing the judgment and decree dated 29-10-1991 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Patuakhali in Title Suit No. 111 of 1987. 

 3. The facts, leading to the filing of these appeals, in short, are that Abdul Motaleb and 36 others as the plaintiffs instituted the instant suit for declaration of their title in the suit land described in the schedule to the plaint. The land covering an area of 43 acres appertaining to RS Khatian No. 157 originally belonged to Lamio Matbar to the extent of 8 annas share and Khemari Mongi and Chamakhi Mongi to the extent of 2 and 6 annas shares respectively. The Revenue Officer by an order dated 3-4-1953 made 17.79 acres of land as khas out of the share belonging to Lamio Matbar in Miscellaneous Case No. 9 of 1952 under section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the remaining .372 acre was duly recorded in his name in SA Khatian No. 240. The shares of Khemari and Chamakhi Mongi were recorded in the SA Khatian No. 142. Against the decision of making khas, Lamio Matbar preferred an appeal before the learned Special Judge, Bakergonj, who on consideration of the evidence on record set aside the order passed by the Revenue Officer. The Additional Collector, Bakergonj by an order dated 12-7-1955 in Miscellaneous Case No. 192/55-56 directed to realize the rent from Lamio Matbar for those lands. He also directed not to disturb the possession of Lamio Matbar in those 17.79 acres of land. Subsequently, the Revenue officer corrected the Khatian in Miscellaneous Case No. 30 of 1977-78. The plaintiffs purchased the suit land from Lamio Matbar and had their names recorded in the khatian between 1956 and 1963. In 1987 some of the defendants claimed that they had taken settlement of the suit land from the Government denying the title of the plaintiffs to the suit land and hence the plaintiffs have been constrained to file the aforesaid suit. 

 4. The Defendants filed three sets of written statements. Their case, in essence, is that suit land is khas land of the Government which settled the same to the defendants in different settlement cases and they have been in possession of the suit land by paying rent to the Government regularly. Defendant Nos. 4 to 11 also stated in their written statement that the suit land is the khas land of the Government which settled 13.03 acres of land to these defendants who are landless cultivators and on the contrary the plaintiffs have no title to, and possession in, the suit land. Defendant Nos. 25 to 28 also filed a separate written statement but ultimately did not contest the suit. 

 6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the trial Court, the plaintiffs (respondents herein) preferred Title Appeal No. 116 of 1992, the Government preferred Title Appeal No. 5 of 1992 and some of the defendants preferred Title Appeal No. 87 of 1992. 

 7. All those appeals were analogously heard and disposed of by the learned Additional District Judge, Patuakhali, who by the judgment decree dated 4-5-1998 allowed the Title Appeal Nos. 87 of 1992 and 5 of 1992 and dismissed the Title Appeal No. 116 of 1992 and set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and also dismissed the suit as a whole. 

 12. We have considered the impugned judgment delivered by the High Court Division and the other papers in the paper book. Admittedly, the suit land along with other lands originally belonged to Lamio Matbar. The Revenue Officer by an order dated 3-4-1953 made 17.79 acres of land khas out of the share belonging to Lamio Matbar in Miscellaneous Case No. 9 of 1952 under section 20 of the State Acquisition of the Tenancy Act (hereinafter referred to as the Act). Against the decision of making khas, Lamio Matbar preferred Special Appeal No. 290 of 1954 before the learned Special Judge, Bakergonj, who on consideration of the evidence on record, set aside the order passed by the Revenue Officer. The Additional Collector, Bakergonj, by an order dated 12-7-1955 in Miscellaneous Case No. 192/55-56 directed to realize rent from Lamio Matbar from those lands. He also directed not to disturb the possession of the Lamio Matbar in those 17.79 acres of land. Subsequently, the Revenue Officer recorded the khatian in Miscellaneous Case No. 30/77-78 in respect of those lands. The plaintiffs purchased the suit land from Lamio Matbar and had their names recorded in the khatian in respect of their purchased land. In 1987 some defendants claimed that they had taken settlement of the suit land from Government denying the title of the plaintiffs. 

 "I. The land in question is the khas land of the Government and the Government settled the same to various defendants and they have been possession the same by paying regular rent and the plaintiffs have no right, title, interest and possession and that the land has been made khas under section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It is argued that the Revenue Officer by order dated 3-4-1953 declared that 17.79 acres of land were the khas land of the original owner Lamio Matbar and the original owner successfully challenged the order in Special Appeal No. 2904 of 1954 before the Special Judge, Bakergonj and the High Court Division committed an error in arriving at a finding that since the revenue authority did not take any action as per direction of the Special Judge and accepted rent from the original owners, they have acquired right, title and interest. It is further argued that the original owner did not challenge the judgment and order passed by the Special/Subordinate Judge before the higher Court and the same is binding upon the revenue authority as well as the original owner and the revenue authority has no power to pass any order for collection of rent from the original owner and that the High Court Division having considered that the schedule and the provision of section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act declared that the suit is the khas land of the Government and has accordingly been recorded in khatian No. 1 Lamio Matbar ceased to have any right, title and interest in the same land and, as such, the transferee from him has acquired no right, title and interest." 

 "(4) The Government may appoint one or more persons who has or have exercised the power of a District Judge or a Subordinate Judge to be a Special Judge or Special Judges for the purposes of hearing appeals which may be preferred to him or them under the provisions of this Act and of inquiring into disputes as to the title to receive any compensation under a Compensation Assessment-roll finally published under section 42 or as to the apportionment of any compensation referred to him under section 60. 

 "When a District Judge has been defined as "the Judge of a Principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction" by using this expression for constituting the election appellate tribunal and empowering to hear him an appeal from the decision of an Election Tribunal, it can not be intended that he is to act as a 'persona designata'. While making such legislation the law-making authority is supposed to know the definition of such expression provided in existing Act. Also, from the very context in which it has been used, it is evident that District Judge is not to act in his private capacity or any capacity other than a Court. This would appear from the qualifying words "within whose jurisdiction the election in dispute was held" used in Article (section) 29(4) of the Ordinance. The qualifying words exclude any other capacity which may be attributed to him, obviously enough such jurisdiction means and refers to the jurisdiction he exercises while sitting as a Court." 

 25. Sub-section 1 of section 39 laid down that compensation payable to a rent receiver, a cultivating raiyat, a cultivating under raiyat or a non-agricultural tenant, in respect of the acquisition of lands in his khash possession which he is not entitled to retain under section 20, shall be determined in accordance with the table mentioned in section 39. Sub-section 2 of section 39 then states that said that any dispute regarding classification of the lands for the purpose of sub-section 1 shall be referred to the prescribed revenue authority whose decision thereon shall be final. Section 40 deals with preliminary publication of Compensation Assessment-roll and then section 41 deals with appeal which can be presented with regard to assessment of compensation against the decision of the revenue authority. It is after all these that under section 42 the final publication of Compensation Assessment-roll is made. Section 44 then says that on the publication of a notification in the official gazette under sub-section 2 of section 43 declaring that compensation mentioned in that section shall ensue, one of them, being that all the interests that are acquirable under the Act but have not acquired under Chapter-II of the Act shall "with the effect from the fist day of the agricultural year next following the date of publication of such notification in the Official Gazettee, be deemed to have been acquired by the Government and vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances".
justice_names: Mr. Justice Muhammad Mamataz Uddin Ahmed

parties:
Harun-or-Rashid ------ Appellant 
VS
Gulaynoor Bibi and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Muzammel Hossain J: This appeal by leave is directed against the judgment and order dated 11-4-2005 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3951 of 2003 discharging the Rule upon affirming the order No. 386 dated 11-8-2003 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 88 of 1994 allowing an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure,1908 reversing his earlier order dated 8-6-2003 rejecting the amendment applications dated 2-2-2003 and 6-5-2003 which were earlier allowed on 8-6-2003. 

 2. The facts for disposal of this appeal, in short, are that one Mirza Md Ashraf instituted Title Suit No.353 of 1974 in the Court of the learned Munsif, 1st Court, Dhaka for declaration of title in the suit property as described in the schedule to the plaint. The suit was subsequently transferred to the Court of learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka, now the Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka and renumbered as Title Suit No. 88 of 1994. 

 3. During pendency of the suit the plaintiff Nos. 2-14, the purchasers in possession of the suit land from the original plaintiffs were added as plaintiff Nos. 16-65 who are also the subsequent purchasers in possession of the suit land. 

 4. The original plaintiff, Mirza Md Ashraf died in 1981 leaving behind his legal heirs who were substituted on his behalf as plaintiff Nos.1(kha)-1(jha) in 1984. The suit property was recorded in the name of the added plain-tiffs along with the original plaintiffs in RS record. The added plaintiff Nos. 2-29 and 33-53 brought an application dated 2-2-2003 and another application dated 6-5-2003 under Order VI, rule 17 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for amendment of the plaint and also for marking the deed dated 6-9-1971 as an exhibit in place of the earlier document. 

 "i. That the impugned judgment and order dated 11-4-2005 passed by the High Court Division being erroneous, illegal and perverse cannot be sustained in law in the facts and circumstances of the case; that the learned Judge of the High Court Division on perusal of the applications for amendment under Order VI, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure Annexure-A and A(1) found that those applications have been brought by the added plaintiffs who are RS recorded tenants and in possession of the suit land as purchaser from the original owner and they were added long before the substitution of the heirs of the original plaintiff; that the defendant-petitioner have every right to make necessary amendment in the plaint if the same does not change the nature and feature of the suit land; that the learned Judge of the High Court Division committed error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice by discharging the Rule against the order of cancellation of the order of amendment; 

 iii. that the High Court Division having found 'the same Court while allowing applications for amendment vide its earlier order dated 8-6-2003 found that the amendment will not affect the nature and feature of the suit, has committed error of law by discharging the Rule by holding in such view of the matter I find no merit in the Rule which is liable to be discharged, and this being self-contradictory, the judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be set-aside; that the added plaintiffs having acquired title from the original owner plaintiff, Mirza Ashraf and they being in possession of the suit land have every right to make necessary amendment in the plaint without changing nature and feature of the plaint but the learned Joint District Judge has illegally cancelled his earlier order of amendment wrongly holding that the plaint can be amended only by the original plaintiff or his substituted plaintiffs and none else; 

 iv. that the original owner namely the plaintiff, Mirza Md Ashraf having sold his entire interest in the suit land before his death in 1981 his heirs, the substituted plaintiffs did not get any interest in the suit land and, as such, their names were not recorded in Mahanagar Settlement Operation; that the order of the High Court Division discharging the Rule in Civil Revision is erroneous and perverse in the facts and circumstances of the case and is liable to be set-aside for the ends of justice." 

 9. Mr Bivash Chandra Biswas, the learned Advocate-on-Record appearing on behalf of the respondent Nos.1-17 submits that there is no illegality in the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division in discharging the Rule because the case of the co-plaintiffs cannot be amended by way of amendment, the original plaintiffs will be seriously prejudiced and as a result the trial Court vacated the earlier order of the amendment of plaint. He then submits that since the co-plaintiffs have stepped into the shoes of the original plaintiffs and if the amendment is not made for the benefit of all the plaintiffs then that cannot be allowed and in that view of the matter the High Court Division rightly discharged the Rule and, as such, the appeal is liable to be dismissed. 

 12. The substituted plaintiff Nos.1(kha)- 1(kha), heirs of the original plaintiffs brought an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 5-7-2003 for reconsideration of its earlier order dated 8-6-2003 which was contested by the added plaintiff Nos. 2-29 and 33-53. The learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka by the order No. 386 dated 11-8-2003 allowed the application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and thereby earlier order dated 8-6-2003 has been recalled. 

 13. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid order dated 11-8-2003 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, plaintiff-petitioner, Harun-or-Rashid preferred revisional application before the High Court Division and a Single Bench of the High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order dated 11-4-2005 discharged the Rule observing that adding of the plaintiffs who are the purchasers from the original plaintiffs remains unchallenged by the revisional petitioner. It appears that the High Court Division also observed that the same Court while allowing the application for amendment by order dated 8-6-2003 found that the amendment will not affect the nature and feature of the suit and accordingly High Court Division did not find any merit in the Rule and in the result the Rule was discharged. 

 14. The pertinent question in the instant case before us is whether the High Court Division is correct in passing the impugned judgment and order dated 11-4-2005 in discharging the Rule upon affirming the judgment and order dated 11-8-2003 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No.88 of 1994 allowing the application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and reversing the earlier order dated 8-6-2003 rejecting the application for amendment.

parties:
Manzur Ahmed ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakkha (RAJUK) & other ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
2. Short fact, as appear from the relevant documents annexed to the writ petition, are that the land and the building thereon at plot No. N(W)H, Block-6, 159 Gulshan Avenue, Gulshan-2, Dhaka (hereinafter called "the said property") originally belonged to one Mrs lnge Flatz (an Austrian Lady) by virtue of a lease deed dated 14-9-1965 executed by the then Dhaka Improvement Trust (DIT) in her favour for 99 years. After Liberation, since the said property became abandoned under the provisions of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 ("PO 16 of 1972"), the said Lady applied to the Government for release of the same on the plea that it was wrongly vested as abandoned property whereupon the government divested the said property, executed a registered sale Deed in her favour on 21-6-1980, and accordingly restored her possession. The said Lady, thereafter, executed an Agreement for Sale on 10-8-1985 through her constituted Attorney, Mr Mohasin Darbar, agreeing to sell the said property in favour of the petitioner upon receiving certain portion of consideration money and put him in possession. However, since she failed to execute the registered sale deed as per the sale agreement, the petitioner filed a spit for specific performance of contract before the First Subordinate Judge, Dhaka which was subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No.279 of 1999 being transferred to the then Additional Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. The suit was contested by RAJUK (defendant No.3) but not by the Government (defendant No. 2). Never the less, the trial Court having dismissed the suit, the petitioner preferred First Appeal No.585 of 2001 before the High Court Division which was contested by Government, but not by RAJUK. The High Court Division, upon hearing the contesting parties, decreed the suit by judgment and Decree dated 15- 12-2005 and, consequently, directed the Government to execute and register a sale deed in favour of the petitioner within 60 days as it transpired, at the time of appeal-hearing, that the said property had in the meantime vested in the Republic in view of Article 143 of the Constitution because of the death of the said Lady intestate and her attorney. In the said decree, the High Court Division further direct- ed respondent RAJUK "to accord necessary permission receiving the legal transfer fee as per consideration money within the date for facilitating the execution and registration of the sale deed in default of which the plaintiff shall be at liberty to get the sale deed executed and registered through Court in accordance with law". RAJUK's belated attempt to have this decree set-aside by the Appellate Division (in Civil petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2027 of 2008) having been failed, the petitioner filed execution case and got the registered sale deed executed on 24-9-2006 in his favour through the executing court. Accordingly, the petitioner submitted application before the RAJUK to have the said property mutated in his name upon payment of transfer fee as per the terms of the said decree, but the RAJUK having refused to do so, he has moved this Court and obtained the Rule. 

 5. Mr Moudud Ahmed submits that the property in question admittedly belonged to the said Austrian Lady under a registered leased deed executed by the then DIT. He argues that although the said property once vested in the Government Wrongly, the Government, upon rectifying the mistake, divested the same and accordingly executed a registered sale deed on 21-06-1980 in favour of the said Lady and restored her possession. Referring to several letters of the Government and RAJUK at the relevant time (Annexures- X-1 to X-5 to the petitioner's Affidavit-in-Reply), he submits that after such sale deed and restoration of possession neither the Government nor the RAJUK can now take advantage of the said 'Ka' list merely because the Government mistakenly included the said property in it. He argues that after such sale, the said lady became the absolute lease-hold owner of the said property subject to the terms of the sale deed and after that she executed the said agreement for sale on 10-8-1985. Therefore, he submits, even if the said property is included subsequently in the list published under the said Ordinance, the same is the result I of non-application of mind by the Government official and a mistake on the face of it and, as such, will carry no legal consequence. He alternatively argues that since the possession of the said property was never taken by the Government after he said sale, inclusion of the same in the 'Ka' list is also an act without jurisdiction. According to him since the High Court Division in its judgment passed in First Appeal No. 585 of 2001 directly or indirectly took into consideration all these circumstances and categorically held that the petitioner had been able to prove all relevant documents including the sale deed executed by the Government (Exhibit- 2) and accordingly directed RAJUK to mutate the said property in his favour, the petitioner has acquired a legally enforceable right and, as such, he is entitled to the directions in the form of mandamus from this Court under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. 

 8. It appears that there is no dispute as to the initial title of the original lease-hold owner, the Austrian Lady. Several matters and papers relied upon by the parties in this case have been proved in the aforementioned Title Suit by the judgment and decree passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 545 of 2001. The admitted position is that after the independence of Bangladesh in 1971, the said property vested in the Government by operation of the provisions of PO 16 of 1972. After such vesting, the original owner filed an application before the Government to release her property on the plea the same was wrongly vested. Upon this, the Government by letter dated 13-5-1980 (Annexure-X-1 to the Affidavit-in-Reply) informed the said Lady Its decision to divest the said property in her favour. Relevant portion of the said letter is quoted below: 

 Subject : Restoration of abandoned house No. NW (H)-6, Road No. 159, Gulshan Avenue, Dacca to its original owner Mrslnge Flatz an Austrian citizen.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 382 of 2009
parties:
Munshi Abdul Hai ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Sanjoy Kumar Shil ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
Shah Abu. Nayeem Mominur Rahman J:- Instant application under Article 103 of the Constitution is for granting leave to appeal against the judgment and order dated 27.10.2008 making the Rule absolute issued in Civil Revision No. 1827 of 2004 by the High Court Division and thereby setting aside the judgment and decree dated 29.03.2004 allowing the Title Appeal No. 89 of 2001 by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Laxmipur, by which the judgment and decree dated 26.06.2001 decreeing the Title Suit No.88 of 2000 by the learned Assistant Judge, Ramganj, Laxmipur, was reversed. 

 2. The respondent hereof as plaintiff filed the Title Suit No.88 of 2000 for declaration that the Mutation Khatian No. 270 was illegal, inoperative and collusive and made behind his back con-tending, inter alia, that the said Khatian has been prepared in the name of the defendant-petitioner hereof having no right, title and interest or possession in the suit land and that the suit land measuring 57 decimals of land out of 5.50 acres appertaining D.S. Khatian No.  82 corresponding to M. R.R Khatian No. 134 originally belonged to three sons of Doyaram Shil and that the said three sons while owning and possessing the suit land, one of them named Balaram Shil died leaving behind his other two brothers, namely, Rarnkanai Shil and R. amkumar Shil, who being the legal heirs and successor-in-interest inherited Balaramrs share. Subsequently Ramkumar Shil died leaving behind two sons namely, Kalinath Shil and Jadunath Shil to inherit his share and that Jadunath Shil died leaving behind one son Kcshab Chandra Shil and that the plaintiff Sanjoy Kumar Shil by virtue gift deeds dated 01.06.1992 and 28.06.1993 from the legal heirs in succession became owner possessor of 81 decimals of land including the suit land by erecting dwelling house as well as by growing seasonal crops thereon and that the impugned mutation khatian having been created, without notice, collusively in the name of the defendant-petitioner, the plaintiff-respondent has been compelled to file the suit. 

 5. After discussing the evidence and the materials on record the trial Court decided the issues and accordingly decreed the suit declaring that the impugned orders relating to mutation in respect of the suit land are illegal, without jurisdiction and void holding, amongst others, that the plaintiff has proved his title and possession in the suit land and that the suit land is not a vested or non-resident property and that the sale vide. deed dated 28.10.1970 could-not be executed or registered by Jadhunath Shil since he died in the year 1968 as has been proved by P. W.2 and D.,W,.2 and that in-spite of Court's direction the defendant failed to produce his title deed in respect of the suit property and that the plaintiff by submitting the original gift deed proved his title, which fact was also corroborated by P.W.2, a teacher of a High School, and D.W.2, the Chairman in charge of the Union Parishad, and that the suit was filed within limitation and is maintain-able. 

 6. Being aggrieved there-against the defendant preferred Title Appeal No. 89 of 2001 in the Court of District Judge, Laxmipur, and the said appeal on transfer was heard and disposed of by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Laxmipur, allowing the appeal and thereby dismissing the suit setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court holding that the suit was not maintainable and the suit was bad for defect of party and that the decision of the trial Court that the sale deed dated 28.10.1970, on the basis which of the defendant claims title and possession, was not executed and registered by Jadhunath Shil and therefore is without any basis and that the suit is bad for defect of parties since the officials of the Revenue Department were not impleaded in the suit. 

 "The Court of appeal below on a misconception of law held that since the plaintiff was not a party in the order mutating the name of the defendant, he was not entitled to challenge that order in failing to consider that the defendant mutated his name in respect of the suit land over Which the plaintiff had acquired right and interest and that the said ex-parte order adversely affected his interest in the suit land and therefore, the plaintiff had the locus standi to challenge this order of mutating the name of the defendant. 

 The Court of appeal below further observed that the suit is bad for defect of party in the absence of the Revenue Officer; this observation is also based upon misconception of law, inasmuch as, the Revenue Officer has passed the order while performing his official works and therefore the Revenue Officer having no subsisting interest in the suit land is neither a necessary nor a proper party in the suit. The Court of appeal below further held that the defendant having informed the Court that he had transferred the suit land in favour of Foriduddin, the suit without him is not maintainable. This observation of the Court of appeal below is based upon conjectures and surmises, inasmuch as, the defendant has not appeal below failed to notice that a partition suit is filed against a co-sharer but the defendants are not co-sharers in the suit land; they have no semblance of title in the suit land. This finding is based on hypothesis. The Court of appeal below further held that the suit with lit seeking declaration of title is not legally maintainable. The Court of appeal below failed to consider that the learned Assistant Judge on consideration of the oral and documentary evidence on record held that the plaintiff has been able to prove his title and possession in the suit land. The Court must have regard to all relevant allegations in the plaint and must look to the Substance of the matter and not its form. Though the plaintiff does not seek declaration of title, if the plaint as a whole is read together it will appear that the plaintiff in fact is seeking title in the suit lands and accordingly, the trial Court has declared plaintiffs title and possession in exercise of powers under Order 7 Rule 7 C.P.C. under this provision a plaintiff ought to be given such relief as he is entitled to get on the facts established upon the evidence in the case even if the plaintiff does not contain a specific prayer for the relief. The judgment of the Court of appeal below is not only based upon misreading and non-consideration of the evidence on record, but the same is also based upon conjectures and surmises. He has made some observations without having no basis at all as there is no material on record in support of such observation. The Court of appeal below has made out a third case in finding about non-existence of Keshab and also in finding about non-maintainability of the suit. The Court of appeal below also did not reverse all the findings arrived at by the trial-Court and in that view of the matter; the judgment of the Court of appeal below is not a proper judgment of reversal."
justice_names: Mr. Justice Shah Abu Nayeem Mominur Rahman
