parties:
Johura Khatun and others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Sajed Ali Khan & others  ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
The certified copy of the plaint of Title Suit No. 309 of 2004 and the Order dated 13-8-2005 passed by the Joint District Judge, First Court Dhaka be kept with the record. 

 2. In an application under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure leave was granted to examine the legality and propriety of the impugned judgment and Order passed by the revisional Court dated 5-2-2008 in Civil Revision No. 191 of 2007 reversing the judgment and Order: dated 31-5-2007 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, 6th Court Dhaka in Title Suit No. 17 of 2006 in rejecting the application for rejection of plaint. 

 3. The predecessor in interest of the present opposite parties as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 7 of 1956 for partition which was subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No. 49 of 1957 and lastly Title Suit No. 68 of 2003 now pending before the Joint District Judge, Dhaka wherein the predecessor in interest of the petitioners are different. The defendants contested the suit and ultimately the trial Court after hearing the parties, considering the facts and circumstances, provision of law, evidence both oral and documentary decreed the suit in preliminary form vide judgment and decree dated 20-2-1959. Being aggrieved the predecessor in interest of the present petitioners i.e. the defendants of the aforesaid suit preferred Appeal being First Appeal No. 179 of 1959. However, the appellate Court affirmed the decree with some modification. Thereafter, the trial Court proceeded with the suit and the same is now pending. The present petitioner as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 17 of 2006 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka for a declaration that the judgment and decree in preliminary form passed in Title Suit No. 49 of 1957 is obtained by practicing fraud upon the Court as well as the defendants. The defendants opposite party entered appearance and filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejecting of the plaint. The trial Court after hearing the parties, considering the facts and circumstances and the plaint vide judgment and Order dated 31-5-2007 rejected the application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and directed the defendants to file written statement. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and Order passed by the trial Court the opposite party as petitioner invoked section 115 (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure before the District Judge, Dhaka being Civil Revision No. 191 of 2007 and the same was heard and disposed of by the District Judge who vide the impugned judgment and Order allowed the said revision and thereby allowed the application for rejection of plaint by setting aside the judgment and Order passed by the trial Court. 

 6. Mr Lutfor Rahman Mondal, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that the revisional Court without applying its judicial mind and without considering the facts arid circumstances and the provisions of law specially by misinterpreting the provision relates to rejection of plaint, limitation etc, most illegally and in an unlawful manner passed the impugned judgment and Order and thereby the revisional Court committed an error of an important question of law occasioning failure of justice. He submits that the revisional Court on misconception and by misinterpretation of the law and relevant provisions relates to rejection of plaint most illegally and in an arbitrary manner passed the impugned judgment and Order which is liable to be set aside for ends of justice. The learned Advocate frankly submits that the petitioners contesting the original suit and also filed an Appeal unsuccessfully. He also submits that the petitioner preferred Title Suit No. 309 of2004, plaint of which has been rejected but in the present case in hand the petitioner raises the practice of fraud only in such circumstances the suit is not barred under any law of limitation. Referring the decision reported in 13 BLD (AD) 217 and 11 MLR (AD) 58 he submits that the question of res judicata is to be considered by the Court below very carefully. Referring the decision reported in 32 DLR (AD) 167 as well as 19 DLR (SC) 433 he submits that in the case of practice of fraud the limitation shall run from date of actual knowledge of such practice of fraud. He submits that the revisional Court ought to have considered the complicated question of fraud raised by the petitioner in the present suit thus the Courts below committed an error of an important question of law occasioning failure of justice. 

 7. I have perused the impugned judgment and Order, Order passed by the trial Court, supplementary affidavit annexures, and the plaint of Title Suit No. 309 of 2004 as well as the Order dated 13-8- 2005. 

 8. On perusal of the same it appears that a partition suit was initiated in the year 1956 being Title Suit No.7 of 1956 and the same is still pending for final disposal. In the said suit the trial Court passed the preliminary decree in the year 1956 and the same challenged by the present petitioner by way of Appeal and the appellate Court however affirmed the same. The trial Court proceeded with the same and the same is now pending being Title Suit No. 68 of 2003. 

 9. Admittedly the petitioner filed a suit challenging the aforesaid decree being Title Suit No. 309 of 2004 wherein the ground pressed by the petitioner is the ground of adverse possession. Raising the question of adverse possession the petitioner in that suit challenged the legality and property of the original decree and the Trial Court rejected the plaint. 

 10. The petitioner thereafter preferred the present suit namely Title Suit No. 17 of 2006 raising the question of fraud. The defendants opposite party filed an application for rejection of plaint before the trial Court unsuccessfully but ultimately the plaint was rejected by the revisional Court. 

 11. On perusal of the impugned judgment and Order passed by the revisional Court it appears that the revisional Court rejected the plaint mainly on the ground of limitation, rejection of Title Suit No. 309 of2004 in earlier occasion as well as preferring First Appeal being No. 179 of 1956 by the present petitioner. 

 14. It is admitted position, that the present petitioner contested the original suit, preferred appear as well as preferred Title Suit No. 309 of 2004 i.e. the present petitioners are aware of the proceeding. 

 15. On perusal of the judgment passed by this Court in Civil Order No. 1465 of 2007 it appears that the petitioner also filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the trial Court in Title Suit No. 68 of 2003 for setting aside the preliminary decree in the original on the allegation of fraud. The trial Court however rejected the application and the first revisional Court affirmed the same. Being aggrieved the petitioner preferred revision before this Court under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure which was rejected summarily. In the said Order the High Court Division held as follows: 

 "When the remedy available to the defendants has been availed of by filing Title Suit No. 17 of 2006 for setting the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 7 of 1956 on the ground of fraud in obtaining the said decree the revisional Court accordingly not allow such prayer and by the impugned Order dated 4-3-2007 - rejected Civil Revision No. 277 of 2006." 

 19. So it is apparent from the record that the trial Court in Title Suit No. 68 of2003 found prima facie case of fraud. 

 20. Since the present petitioner filed the suit for setting aside of the preliminary decree absolutely on different ground of fraud at this stage it cannot be said that the plaint is barred by Order VII, rule 11 (d) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Regarding the limitation it is now a well settled proposition of law is that the limitation shall run from the date of actual knowledge and in the case in hand the period of' limitation is very much in favour of the petitioner. The question of fraud is being raised in the suit and the same question was neither raised by the petitioner in Appeal or in Title Suit No. 309 of 2004. In such circumstances it cannot be said outright that the present suit is hit by doctrine of resiudicata. Obviously the trial Court by framing issues regarding res judicata and limitation can dispose of the suit after taking evidence after commending the facts and circumstances. The decisions as referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioner lend support to above contention.

parties:
Bangladesh ----- Petitioner
vs
Rafeda Khatun and ors ----- Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
2. The opposite-parties as plaintiffs instituted other Class Suit No.2 of 2004 in the Court of Joint District Judge, First Court Mymensingh for declaration of title in respect of the suit land. 

 3. Plaintiffs' case, in short, was that the nature of the suit land was homestead and pond and it belonged to Maharaja Sitangshu Kumar Acharjee Chowdhury. The predecessor of the plaintiffs, Abdul Hye Sujan took rokka pattan of the suit land on 18th Kartic 1351 BS and since then he had been in possession therein by constructing dwelling house, excavating pond and rearing fish. Preliminary record of right was prepared in the name of Abdul Hye Sujan, but finally was prepared in the name of the Government. Said Abdul Hye Sujan died on 30-9-1996 leaving behind the plaintiffs as his legal heirs. Thus the predecessor of the plaintiffs and after his death the plaintiffs had/have been possessing the suit land for more than 60 years. The plaintiffs came to know about the wrong recording of the record of right in the name of the Government for the first time on 2-5-2002 which created, cloud over their title to the suit land, hence the suit. 

 4. Defendants contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit land belonged to Zaminder and CS Khatian was prepared in the name of Zaminder and by operation of law the same vested in the Government after the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (the Act) came into being. Record of right was correctly prepared in 1962 in the name of the Government. Further case of the defendants was that the plaintiffs had/have no right, title and interest in the suit land. In order to grab the suit land of the Government plaintiffs created some false documents and instituted the present suit. 

 5. At the trial the plaintiffs examined 5 witnesses and filed some documents in support of their claim to the suit land. The defendants examined one witness and also filed documents. The learned Joint District Judge on consideration of the evidence on record by his judgment and decree dated 31-8-2005 decreed the suit declaring the plaintiffs' title to the suit land. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said judgment and decree of the trial Court the defendants preferred other Appeal No. 250 of 2005 before the District Judge, Mymensingh the said appeal on being transferred was heard and disposed of by the Additional District Judge, Second Court, Mymensingh who by the impugned judgment and decree dismissed the appeal affirming those passed by the trial Court. Hence this revision by defendant No.1. 

 6. Mr Zainul Abedin, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, appearing for the petitioner, submitted that the Courts below failed to consider the interpolation in the alleged rokka pattan, the very basis of the plaintiffs' claim which was admitted by PW 5, Mohini Mohan Dey and non consideration of the said apparent factual aspect and the evidence of PW 5 resulted in an error occasioning failure of justice in decreeing the suit. He further submitted that the suit land belonged to Zaminder Maharaja Sitangshu Kumar Acharjee Chowdhury as khash land. After the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into force the suit land, being chandina land, vested in the Government as khash land. Accordingly, record of right was correctly prepared in the name of the Government. Therefore, by the alleged pattan the plaintiffs' predecessor did not acquire any title to the suit land, both the Courts below committed error of law resulting in an error occasioning failure of justice in decreeing the suit and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set aside. 

 7. Mr Sikder Mahmudur Raji, the learned Advocate appearing with Mr Md Bakiruddin Bhuiyan for the plaintiff-opposite-parties, on the other hand, submitted that the predecessor of the plaintiffs took rokka pattan of the suit land on 18th Kartic, 1351 BS from Maharaja Sitangshu Kumar Acharjee Chowdhury and since then had been possessing peacefully without any interference from any quarter. Accordingly, they acquired valid right, title and interest in the suit land, but the suit land was wrongly recorded as khash land in the record of right in the name of the Government which they came to know on 2-5-2002 and, as such, they instituted the suit for declaration of their title, the court below rightly decreed the suit. He further submitted that both the courts below having concurrently believed plaintiffs' case of settlement by rokka from its original owner and thus title in the suit land there is no scope of interference with the impugned judgment and decree by this Court in exercising revisional jurisdiction and, as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

 10. From Exhibit 3 series it appeared that the suit land is Chandina land, so the same vested in the Government after the acquisition of the wholesale interest of the Zamindars pursuant to the provisions of section 3 of the Act, and therefore, neither the plaintiffs' predecessor nor the plaintiffs did acquire any title in the suit land by virtue of the alleged rokka pattern. From Exhibit 3 series, 'Kha' and 'Ga', it is clear that the suit land is Khas land of the Government. PW 5 Mohini Mohan Dey, who was 92 years old and examined to prove the settlement by the Zamindars, stated in his cross-examination to the effect : “দাখিলাগুলিতে ঘষা মাজা আছে।” We have also perused the dakhila and the same appeared to us interpolated which fact alone created doubt as to the genuineness of the same. But unfortunately, none of the courts below considered the said vital piece of evidence of PW 5 and thus fell into an error in finding title of the plaintiffs in the suit land. It is true that the appellate Court is the last court of fact, but it having failed to consider the material evidence as discussed above, the finding of fact arrived by it is not infallible and can be interfered with in revision. 

 11. Mr Raji relying on the case of Bangladesh vs Har Chandra Nath reported in 10 MLR (AD) 313 tried to argue that the plaintiffs also acquired right, title, and interest in the suit land by virtue of their possession therein for more than 60 years, so the courts below rightly decreed the suit. 

 12. Both the courts below concurrently found that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land for a long continuous period. But the question is, whether they are in possession for more than 60 years, because in order to acquire title by way of adverse possession the plaintiffs must prove their possession for more then 60 years as provided in Article 149 of the Limitation Act, 1908. The rokka pattan by which the plaintiffs' predecessor claimed to have taken pattan though not proved even if taken into consideration for the purpose of possession it appeared that the same is dated 18th Kartic 1351 BS corresponding to 2/3 November, 1944 and the suit was instituted on 2-1-2005, that is, before 60 years. Therefore, the plaintiffs did not acquire any title to the suit land by virtue of their possession. 

 14. In conclusion, we are constrained to hold that the plaintiffs failed to prove their title to the suit land so the court below was not justified in affirming the decree of the trial Court decreeing the suit declaring their title.

parties:
Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakka (RAJUK) -------- Appellant
Vs. 
 Jahan Ara Begum and others -------- Respondents
full_judgment:
3. Facts in all the appeals are more or less same. It was the case of the writ-petitioners that proceeding for the acquisition of the land was initiated and part of the compensation money was paid but later on Government decided to de-requisition their land along with the land of others and thereupon they were served with the notice to return the compensation money received earlier by them and accordingly, they refunded the compensation money to the Deputy Commissioner but in spite of that the deputy commissioner did not complete the process of de-requisition. It was the case of the writ petitioners that they are in possession of the land and that they have exclusive right, title, interest and possession in the land in suit. 

 6. At the time of hearing it was contended on behalf of the writ-petitioners that Government took decision to de-requisition 1005 acres of land out of 2076 acres of land and thereupon issued notice to the writ-petitioners and in some cases to their predecessors-in-interest asking for refund of the compensation money earlier received by the persons whose land were requisitioned and that the petitioners remained in possession of their respective land. It was also contended that some of the writ-petitioners were not paid any compensation in respect of the land so requisitioned. It was further contended that it was the legitimate expectation of the writ-petitioners that as their land would no longer be required by the requiring body they would be allowed to remain in possession of their land or in the alternative they would be provided with alternative plot or that they would get compensation in respect of their land as per provision of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982. It was submitted on behalf of the writ-petitioner in refuting the question of non-maintainability of the writ petition that the writ-petitioners were not challenging the acquisition proceeding but they have come before the Court to establish their claim of being entitled to be treated equally and in accordance with law in the matter of either by allotting to them alternative plots or by giving them compensation as per the present market value and till then their possession in the land in question should not be disturbed. 

 7. On behalf of the RAJUK it was contended that LA Cases were duly initiated after issuance of notice upon the owners of the land in question and that the land in question having been requisitioned upon initiation of the LA cases the same vested to the Government under section 93A of the Town Improvement Act and that there is no provision for releasing the land so vested in the Government or, in other words, so requisitioned and that after requisition the land owners are only entitled to get compensation. 

 9. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case we find that the acquisition proceedings have not yet been completed and the petitioners are very much in possession of the lands in question. We therefore hold that the petitioners are entitled to be equally treated and in accordance with law. In such view of the matter, we hold the petitioners must either be given an alternative plot or will be given sufficient compensation as per provision of Ordinance, 1982. We therefore direct that RAJUK to take all possible steps to complete the proceedings of the LA case in question preferably within 6 months from the date of receipt of this order. 

 10. The respondents are also directed to prove their title and ownership in respect of the lands in question if the respondents by this time were given part compensation money they will get the balance amount of compensation as per provision of the said Ordinance or they may be given alternative plot if no compensation was given. In the meantime, the acquiring authority shall finalise the LA case and till then the petitioners shall not be disturbed of their peaceful possession in any manner." 

 11. Leave was granted to consider the submission of the learned Counsel appearing for the appellants in all the appeals that "the High Court Division erred in law in holding/directing that the writ petitioners be given compensation according to the present market value as provided in the Ordinance, 1982 and that the writ-petitioners will get balance amount of compensation as per provision of the said Ordinance, inasmuch as the requisition and acquisition was initiated and carried out under section 93A of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 and that after repeal of the said provision the pending proceeding would continue in pursuance of section 6 of the General Clauses Act and section 73 (Uma) and 74(2), of the Town Improvement (Amendment) Act XXIX of 1987 and, as such, the provisions of. Ordinance No. II of 1982 have no mariner of application in the matter of assessment payment of compensation. He further submits that the High Court Division erred in law in holding that the writ-petitioners may be given alternative plot if no compensation was given, inasmuch as the issue of alternative plot is not germane/related to requisition/acquisition of land under the Town Improve merit Act, 1953 nor alternative plot is linked with compensation nor the writ-petitioners have any fundamental or legal right to allotment of plot as a necessary corollary to requisition of land and, as such, the direction of the High Court Division is beyond the scope of jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102(2)(a)(i) of the Constitution of Bangladesh. He also submits that the High Court-Division committed illegality in upholding the argument that the writ-petitioners had their legitimate expectation that they would be given alter- native plot because the issue of alternative plot has no direct nexus and is not a necessary corollary to acquisition of land of the petitioner under the provisions of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 and further, that the allotment of land is a distinct policy and procedure under distinct allotment rules having distinct specific criteria for such allotment which is not automatic with acquisition of land and that there is no legitimate expectation where there is element of chance and fulfillment of criteria as per process of evaluation. He also submits that the High Court Division committed illegality in entertaining the writ petitioners' claim of title in the acquired property on the basis of transactions subsequent to the requisition process because the original owner/awardee, after the requisition' had no saleable/transferable title in the property and the writ petitioners had no legal right to make any grievance under Article 102(2)(a)(i) of the Constitution before the High Court Division. The learned Counsel further submits that the High Court Division committed illegality in reopening the factual and procedural aspects of LA case No. 138 of 1961-62, inasmuch as those issues had been finally settled by the High Court Division in the case reported in 46 DLR 205 and the said judgment had been affirmed by the Appellate Division, Supreme Court of Bangladesh in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 117-119 of 1994, there was no scope to reagitate those issues. He further submits that the High Court Division in exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 102(2)(a)(i) of the Constitution of Bangladesh traveled beyond the Rule Nisi in granting relief which is neither germane nor has any nexus with impugned public notice published in daily news- papers inviting application for allotment of land to person affected by the acquisition. The learned Counsel lastly submits that the High Court Division committed illegality in failing to hold that the writ petitions as framed challenging a public notice published in national dailies were not maintainable under Article 102(2)(a)(i) of the Constitution (mandamus), inasmuch as writ-petitioners have no fundamental or legal right in non-publication of the public notice nor there is any corresponding statutory obligation upon the appellant (RAJUK) respondent in writ petition) not to publish such public notice and that the said issue of non maintainability has been affirmatively held by the High Court Division in the judgment passed in the Writ Petition No. 4890 of 1996 dated 1-3-2001 by another Division Bench of the High Court Division. 

 12. Mr TH Khan, learned Counsel, appearing for the appellant, submitted that the writ-petitioners be given compensation according to the present market value as provided in the Ordinance, 1982 and that the writ-petitioners will get balance amount of the compensation as per provision of the said Ordinance, inasmuch as the requisition and acquisition was initiated and made under section 93A of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 and that after repeal of the said provision the pending proceeding would continue in pursuance of section 6 of the General Clauses Act and section 73(Uma) and 74(2) of the Town Improvement (Amendment) Act, XXIX of 1987 and, as such, the provisions of Ordinance No. 11 of 1982 have no manner of application in the matter of assessment/payment of compensation; that the writ-petitioners may be given, alternative plot if no compensation was given inasmuch as the issue of alternative plot is not germane/related to requisition/ acquisition of land under the Town Improvement Act, 1953 nor alternative plot is linked with compensaion nor the writ petitioner has any fundamental or legal right to allotment of plot as a necessary corollary of requisition of land, as such, the High Court Division is beyond the scope of jurisdiction under Article 102(2)(a)(i) of the Constitution of Bangladesh; that the writ-petitioners had their legitimate expectation that they would be given alternative plot because the issue of alternative plot has no direct nexus and is not a necessary corollary to acquisition of land of the petitioner under the provisions of Town Improvement Act, 1953 and further, that the allotment of land is a direct policy and procedure under distinct specific criteria for such allotment which is not automatic with acquisition of land and that there is no legitimate expectation where there is element of chance and fulfilment of criteria as per process of evaluation; that the High Court Division committed' illegality in entertaining the writ petitioner's claim of title in the acquired property on the basis of transactions subsequent to the requisition process because the original owner/ awardee, after the requisition had no saleable/transferable title in the property and the writ petitioners had no legal right to make any grievance under Article I02(2)(a)(i) of the Constitution; that the High Court Division committed illegality in reopening the factual and procedural aspects of LA Case No. 138 of 1961-62 inasmuch as those issues had been finally settled by the High Court Division in the case reported in 46 DLR 205 and the said judgment had been affirmed by this Division. The learned Advocate further submitted that the writ- petition as framed challenging a public notice published in national dailies was not maintainable under Article 102(2)(b)(i) of the Constitution, inasmuch as writ petitioner has no fundamental or legal right in non-publication of the public notice nor there is any corresponding statutory obligation upon the appellant not to publish notice and that, the said notice of non-maintainability has been affirmatively held by the High Court Division; that if the compensation is not paid in full the balance of amount to be paid at the rate of present market value, inasmuch as the compensation has already been paid to the actual owners and the same was paid as per relevant law rule existing at the relevant time. 

 14. Dr M Zahir, learned Counsel, appearing for respondent while supporting the impugned judgment and order has, however, submitted that the High Court Division considering the facts and circumstances of the case as represented by the writ- petitioners held that the writ-petitioners are not challenging the acquisition proceeding but alleged to be in their possession of the land-in-question that the writ-petitioners had their legitimate expectation that they will get alternative plot or provided with sufficient compensation as per provision of Ordinance, 1982 referring to the impugned judgment of the High Court Division. The learned Counsel further submitted that as the writ-petitioner-respondents are very much in possession in the land-in- question they are entitled to be treated equally in accordance with law and, as such, the writ- petitioners are entitled to either an alternative plot or be given sufficient compensation as per provision of Ordinance, 1982. 

 18. The High Court Division has also misconceived the provisions of law in applying the same in respect of the petitioner's case because the respondent's right, title and possession extinguished with the completion of the acquisition proceeding vesting right, title interest and provision in the land under acquisition to the Authority, inasmuch as the ex- owner/awardee has ceased to have any right, title and possession thereto upon acquisition of land.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree (FA) No.104 of 1997.
parties:
Abdul Hai and ors ----- Appellants 
Vs. 
Madhab and ors ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
ATM Fazle Kabir J: This appeal, at the instance of defendant-appellants is preferred against the judgment and decree dated 24-10-1996 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Gazipur in Title Suit No. 1219 of 1985 decreeing the suit for recovery of khas possession by evicting the defendants from the suit property. 

 2. The short facts relevant for the purpose of the appeal are that the plaintiff-respondent brought the original suit for declaration of title, recovery of khas possession and realisation of mesne profits. The case of plaintiff-respondent. in short, is that the lands described in the schedule 'A' and 'B' originally belonged to the owners of the Bhowal Raj Estate managed and controlled by the Bhowal Raj Courts of Wards Estate who donated the same along with some other lands to their family deity Sri Sri Madhab shortly after CS operation. That Bhowal Raj Estate including the debuttar properties were being managed by the Courts of Wards and accordingly, the Manager of the said Estate had been possessing the said proportion by letting out the same to Adhi Bargadars. While the property described in the schedule 'A' and 'B' was under management of the Court of Wards, then the defendant No.1 Md Chand Mia took settlement of suit land as Adhi Bargader by executing a registered Barga rabulyat purported to be lease for 10 years with effect from 1371 BS. Thereafter the plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 198 of 1971 and Title Suit No. 226 of 1971 against the defendant Chand Mia for recovery of khas possession in respect of the properties described in the schedule A and realisation of mesne profits for the property described in the schedule B. These two suits were transferred to the Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka for disposal and were renumbered as Title Suit No. 14 of 1976 and Title Suit No. 12 of 1976 respectively. That the defendant No.1 Chand Mia made appearance in the suit but did not contest in the long run and subsequently the said suits were disposed of and decreed on 26-11-1976 and 24-2-1977 respectively. The defendant No. 1 Chand Mia brought two Miscellaneous cases being Nos. 44 of 1976 and 10 of 1977 to set aside the decrees passed in Title Suit No. 12 of 1976 and Title Suit No. 14 of 1976, but ultimately those two cases were dismissed on 20-8-1977 and 16-7-1977 respectively. Thereafter, the plaintiff respondent filed Execution Case No. 2 of 1977 and Execution Case No. 7 of 1977 for recovery of khas possession and in due course the plaintiff-respondent got recovery of khas possession over the suit property, in due process of law by removing the structures therefrom with the help of police. That one Asraf Ali brought Title Suit No. 31 of 1979, but that Asraf Ali, Kanchan Mia and others took lease of the same plots from the Court of Wards of Bhowal Raj Estate for the period of last four months of 1384 BS. The plaintiff has been in possession of the suit properties through Adhi Bargaders. The defendant Nos. 1 and 3 took lease of the suit land described in schedule-A and B by executing two kabulyats for the year of 1386 BS only but they continued their illegal possession even after expiry of their lease period. The defendant No. 1 along with the vendors of the defendant Nos. 2, 4, 5 and 6 have not given up their illegal possession and they finally refused to give up possession of the property on 11-7-1979. Hence the suit is for recovery of khas possession by evicting the defendants therefrom. 

 That the defendant Nos. 2-4,5,6 and 7 contested the original suit by filing separate written statements. The case of the defendant No. 6 A. Hai in short, is that the suit property originally belonged to Chand Mia and Bashiruddin in equal share and their names were duly recorded in SA Khatian No. 63 in respect of the suit land. While Chand Mia was in possession of the suit property he sold 1.05 acres of land of plat No. 147 to the defendant No.6 A Hai by a registered kabala deed dated 20-6-1976. It is further stated that the suit property never belonged to Sree Sree Modhob and no deed of endorsement was made by the Bhowal Raj Estate. That the defendant No.1 Chand Mia never executed a kabulyat in favour of the Bhowal Raj Estate as its Adhi Bargadar rather, he took settlement of the suit land from the ex-landlords in whose names CS Khatian No. 7 was prepared. That Sri Sri Madhob the Deity of Hindu Community did not acquire any title in respect of the suit land, but the employees of the Bhowal Raj Esstate have created some forged documents in order to grab the property of the defendants as such the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 3. Being aggrieved and dissatisfied by the impugned judgment and decree the defendant appellant preferred this appeal stating that the trial Court committed an error in decreeing the original suit. 

 5. Mr ABM Motiur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant appellants, submits that the alleged kabulyat executed by the defendant Chand Mia is a forged and fabricated document but the learned Subordinate Judge wrongly treated it as genuine. The learned Advocate further submits that the PW 2 admitted in his cross-examination that they took delivery of possession of the suit land by paper transaction but, in fact, they could not recover the suit land. The learned Advocate then submits that the witnesses of the plaintiff have failed to prove his case in spite of the fact the learned Subordinate Judge most illegally decreed the suit by the impugned judgment. The learned Advocate further submits that the suit land was duly recorded in SA Khatian No. 63 in the names of Chand Mia and Bashruddin who are the vendors of the defendant appellant No.6 has proved their possession in the suit land, but the learned Subordinate Judge failed to appreciate the evidenciary value of such documents relating to records of right. The learned Advocate incidentally submits that the scheduled land of the plaint does not tally with the documents relating to alleged gift in the name of the deity made by the plaintiff respondent. It is contended that in the absence of specific land no decree for recovery of possession can be granted, but the learned Subordinate Judge most illegally decreed the suit without considering practical aspect of the law. The learned Advocate cited several rulings reported in 4 DLR 447, 7 DLR 61 and 12 DLR 246 and by referring these decisions the learned Advocate submits that under BT Act oral settlement was permissible, as such there was no necessity of document to create tenancy. In view of the fact defendant Chand Mia, the vendor of the appellant took oral settlement from the original landlord, but the learned Subordinate Judge failed to consider the legal aspect of such oral settlement. 

 6. Mr Md Abdul Haque, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-respondent, submits that it is an admitted fact that the suit property originally belonged to Bhowal Raj Estate and it is also undisputed that CS Khatian No.7 was recorded in respect of properties including the suit land in the name of superior landlords of the Bhowel Raj Estate. The learned Advocate then submits that the suit property was duly recorded in the name of Bhowal Raj Estate managed and controlled by the Court of Wards in SA and RS Khatians. (Exhibits-4 & 4 ka) in the name of Sree Sree Mahdhob and the plaintiff paid rents to the government in respect of the suit land. The learned Advocate incidentally submits that Chand Mia, the vender of the defendant No.6, executed a registered kabulyat as Adhi Bargadar under the plaintiff in the year 1371 BS, as such, the defendant No.6 and his vendor Chand Mia acquired no right, title and interest in the suit property. The learned Advocate further submits that the plaintiff-respondent got the decree in Title Suit No. 12 of 1976 and Title Suit No. 14 of 1976 and they took delivery of possession in the suit property by filing Execution case in due process of law, as such, the learned Subordinate Judge has rightly decreed the suit by the impugned judgment. The learned Advocate finally submits that the defendant No.6 new appellant No. 1 Abdul Hye has claimed 1.05 acres of land, but no document was produced and examined by the defendant in support of his claim in the Court below, as such, this appeal has no substance to interfere in the impugned judgment and accordingly the appeal is liable to be dismissed how lot us examine the evidence on record for its critical analysis. 

 8. PW 1 Lehaz Uddin Prodhan is the Head Assistant of the Court of Wards of Bhowal Raj Estate, who stated that the suit property originally belonged to Bhowal Raj Estate and it was donated to Sree Sree Madhob, the Deity of the Bhowal Raj Estate. It is further stated that the defendant Chand Mia took Adhi Barga of the suit land from the plaintiff-respondent by executing a register Kabulyat in 1371 BS. Thereafter, the plaintiff brought two Title suits against Chand Mia and obtained decree for recovery of possession in the suit land. He denied the suggestion that Chand Mia never executed kabulyat in favour of the Court of Wards. 

 9. PW 2 SMA Kadir is the Assistant Chief Manager of Bhowal Raj Estate, who corroborated the plaintiff's case to the effect that the suit property was duly recorded in the name of the Deity Sri Sri Madhob both in SA and RS Khatians, and the vendor of the defendant-appellant named Chand Mia took settlement some portion of the suit land by executing registered kabulyats on 1-8-1963 (Exhibit-1 series) in favour of Bhowal Raj Estate. In cross, he says that after the abolition of Jamindari in 1950 the government acquired the properties of Bhowal Raj Estate save and except the choiced land and debutter land. He further stated in cross that the vendor of the appellant Chand Mia took Adhi-Barga of the suit land in 1371 BS for ten years and subsequently he was evicted from the suit land through process of law in pursuance of the Execution case. He further stated that they got recovery of possession through paper transaction but, in fact, could not got real possession of the property. On the other hand, the defendant side examined two witnesses. DW 1 Zobed Ali has stated that the suit land originally belonged to Bhowal Raj Estate from whom Chand Mia and Bashir Uddin took Pattan of the suit land and it was recorded in the names of Chand Mia, and Bashir Uddin in SA Khatian No. 63 (Exhibit ka-1). He denied the suggestion that Chand Mia took Barga by executing barga-kabulyat in favour of the Bhowal Raj Estate. But in cross, he says that Chand Mia took Adhi-Barga of the suit land by executing a kubilyat dated 1-8-1963 in favour of Bhowal Raj Estate and he purchased 1.05 acres of land from that Chand Mia. He further says that he cannot say whether the Bhowal Raj Estate obtained a decree for recovery of khas possession by evicting Chand Mia from the suit land. DW 2 Md Khadem Hossain, the Manager of the Court of Wards of the Bhowal Raj Estate, deposed but did not give any material evidence in this case. 

 10. On careful scrutiny of the evidence, of both oral and documentary, it is an admitted fact that the suit property originally belonged to ex-landlord of Bhowal Raj Estate and CS Khatian No.7 was duly prepared in their names including the suit property. There is no denying that the property of Bhowal Raj Estate is now being managed and controlled by the Court or wards in respect of choiced land and debutter properties of Bhowal Raj Estate. It is the definite case of the plaintiff than Chand Mia, the vendor of the defendant No.6, executed a registered kubilyat in favour of Court of Wards of Bhowal Raj Estate in 1371 BS Exhibit 1 is the registered kabilyat dated 1-8-1963 executed by the defendant Chand Mia, which shows that he took Adhi barga in respect of the land of the Deity Sree Sree Madhab from the plaintiff for the period of 10 years including the suit plot No. 147. It appears from the said kabilyat that the suit land belonged to the Deity Sree Sree Madhab under Bhowal Raj Estate managed by the Court of Wards. If we consider the cases of both the defendant appellants as well as the plaintiff-respondent side by side, we find that admittedly the suit land originally belonged to Bhowal Raj Estate. It is also undisputed that the property of Bhowal Raj Estate is being managed and controlled by the Court of Wards. It appears from the registered kabilyat dated 1-8-1963 (Exhibit 1) that the defendant Chand Mia executed the deed for taking Adhi-Barga in respect of the debuttor land belonging to the Deity Sree Sree Madhab under management of the Court of Wards. The defendant-appellant has examined only two witnesses who have tried to say that the kabulyat (Exhibit 1) executed by Chand Mia was never acted upon but it appears from the recitals of the said Kubilyat that the defendant Chand Mia admitted that suit land was debutter property of the Deity Sree Sree Madhab. According to the provision of section 92 of the Evidence Act, the oral evidence is always excluded by the documentary evidence and the oral evidence cannot invalidate the contents of the document unless it is proved to be product of forgery. In the instant case, we find that the plaintiff-respondent filed certified copies of both SA Khatian No. 63 and RS Khatian No. 506 (Exhibit Nos. 4, 4ka) in the Court below in 1973 which show that the suit land was recorded in the name of the Deity Sree Sree Madhab Bigroho and others. On the other hand, the defendant-appellant also filed a certified copy of SA Khatian No. 63 in respect of the same land showing recorded in the name of the defendant Chand Mia. It appears that the defendant-appellant obtained certified copy of SA Khatian No. 63 in the year of 1991. Under such circumstances the learned trial Court should have called for the original Khatian volume in order to compare and find out the genuine one, but the trial Court failed to do so. 

 12. In view of the fact, we are of opinion that the certified copy of the SA Khatian No. 63 (Exhibit Ka-1) in respect of the suit land filed by the plaintiff-respondent appears to be genuine one, which was recorded in the names of the Deity Sree Sree Madhab and original landlords. In view of the fact, we are inclined to hold that plaintiff is still absolute owner of the property on the basis of evidence on record. It is also an admitted fact that the suit land originally belonged to Bhowal Raj Estate managed and controlled by the Court of Wards. It further appears from the certified copy of the decree 14 of 1976 (Exhibit-2) that the plaintiff in the earlier occasion filed a suit for recovery of possession against defendant Chand Mia in respect of suit plot No. 147 and obtained decree. It in further evident in the record that Chand Mia defendant No. 1 filed Miscellaneous case for setting aside the decree of that suit, but it was dismissed. So it is proved from the documentary evidence that the decree of Title Suit No. 14 of 1977 is still binding upon the defendant No. 1 Chand Mia from whom the defendant-appellants allegedly purchased some portion of the suit land subsequent to the decree passed in Title Suit No. 14 of 1976. It is further revealed from the certified copy of the report (Exhibit-gha) of process server dated 2-2-1978 that the process server Shahjahan Gazi handed over the possession of the suit land of plot No. 147 to the plaintiff-respondent in Execution Case No. 7 of 1977. It is evident from the documentary evidences on record that the plaintiff-respondent obtained symbolic possession over the suit property on 2-2-1978 and he filed the instant suit for recovery of khas possession in the year of 1985 within 12 years from date of taking delivery of possession through Court, as such the question of adverse possession claimed by the defendant-appellants does not arise. 

 16. The impugned judgment and decree dated 24-10-1996 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Gazipur in Title Suit No. 1219 of 1985 is hereby confirmed.

parties:
Ashraful Alam ------ Appellant
vs
Md Moniruddin and ors ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
2. Respondent Nos. 1 to 6 as plaintiffs on 14- 2-95 instituted the suit for declaration of title in the suit land on the basis of adverse possession only and also for further declaration that said defendant No. 12 acquired no title or interest in the suit land by deeds being No. 16519 dated 23-12-94 and No. 721 of 13-1-95. 

 3. Plaint case, in short, is that the suit land measuring about 3.5 decimals out of 8.38 decimals of plot No. 4090 appertaining to SA Khatian No. 807 under Kotwali Police Station in the district of Rangpur was originally owned and possessed by one Hafez Mohammad Hossain, predecessor- in-interest of defendant Nos. 1 to 11. After his death, said defendant Nos. 1 to 11 possessed the suit land. There was a big four-roof tin hut with many rooms therein, which were let out to different tenants. Three shops and adjacent vacant land comprising of 3.5 decimals remained abandoned for many years. In the first part of 1979, the plaintiffs entered into said shops with knowledge of the owner and started business first under the name and style "Capital Papers Mart". In spite of said entry by the plaintiffs, the owner did not take any steps for their eviction nor recognise them as tenants. By such uninterrupted possession of the suit land along with' shops they acquired title. 

 4. In 1982, they changed the name of the shops to 'Star Studio'. They got trade licence and paid municipality taxes. Title of the original owners was lost due to their long uninterrupted possession. Defendant Nos. 3 to 6 transferred 2.5 decimals of land by aforesaid deed dated 13-12-94 and 3.5 decimals of land by another deed dated 13-1-95 to defendant No. 12. Then, defendant No. 12 asked them on 15-12-95 to hand over possession, which they declined to. Hence, the suit. 

 5. Defendant No. 12 alone contested the suit by filing a written statement. He contended, inter alia, that Hafez Mohammad Hossain was the original owner in possession of the suit land and he hailed from Keraniganj, Dhaka. He used to possess the suit land through tenants. He died leaving behind defendant Nos. 1 to 11 as his only legal representatives. Abdul Motaleb, father of the plaintiffs, took lease of suit shops at a monthly rental of Taka 125. He first started business of papers under the name and style Capital Paper Mart. But he was very irregular in payment of rent. After the death of Abdul Motaleb, the plaintiffs continued as tenants under Hasna Banu Bibi. In 1982, they changed their business and started business of photo accessories under the name and style 'Star Studio'. Heirs of deceased Hafez Mohammad Hossain transferred the suit land with the shops by two deeds dated 23-12-84 and 13-1-85 to defendant No. 12. After the transfer the plaintiffs became tenants under defendant No. 12. 

 (d) whether the plaintiff acquired any title on the basis of possession? and 

 (e) 	what relief the plaintiffs were entitled to ? 

 9. Plaintiff No.4, Md Kutubuddin was examined as PW 1. In support of the plaint case, he said that the suit land measuring about 3.5 decimals out of 8.38 decimals of land was situated in the south-west of said land. The original owner was Hafez Mohammad Hossain. He died leaving defendant Nos. 1 to 11. There were three rooms in the suit land with a latrine, godown and some vacant land. Entire suit land with the shops remained abandoned. The suit land was situated in the commercial area of the town. They first started papers and stationery business in the name and style of 'Capital Paper Mart' on the suit land in 1979. Since then, they possessed the suit land. Owner did not know when he was dispossessed nor the owner ever tried to evict them from the suit' land. They started business of photo accessories under the name and style 'Star Studio' in 1982. He was a son of Abdul Motaleb who died leaving six sons' as his legal representatives. He denied that his father was a tenant at a monthly rental of Taka 125. He admitted that the defendant instituted SCC Suit being No.4 of 1995 for eviction. 

 17. Ashraful Alam, son of defendant No. 12, Shahidur Rahman, examined him as DW 1. He deposed on behalf of his father by giving power of attorney. In support of his case, he said that they acquired title of the suit land including the shops. He deposed that father of the plaintiff first entered into the shops as tenant under the owner Hafez Mohammad Hossain. After his death, the plaintiffs continued as tenants in the suit shops. After purchase, they requested the plaintiffs for settlement of rent on the basis of fresh contract, which they declined. Ultimately, he instituted SCC Suit No.4 of 1995 for eviction. 

 18. DW 2, Md. Zillur Rahman deposed that he knew the suit property and the parties. The suit property comprised of a big four-roof hut. Some shops were made by partition. There were in total five shops. The original owner possessed the shops through tenants. The suit shop is now 'Star Studio', before it was 'Capital Paper Mart'. Abdul Motaleb, father of the plaintiffs, used to do business in the shops as tenant. The suit shops along with vacant land were transferred to the defendant No. 12. The plaintiffs were tenants under defendant No. 12. 

 22. On above evidence, learned Subordinate Judge found that the plaintiffs were possessing the suit property for more than 12 years without any obstruction and thereby, they acquired title by adverse possession. Upon such view, learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit. 

 23. Only question facing us is, whether the learned Subordinate Judge was justified in decreeing the suit and declaring the title of the plaintiffs in the suit land on the basis of adverse possession. 

 24. As stated above, the plaintiffs instituted the suit for declaration of their title in the suit land by adverse possession. The suit land comprised of a four-roof tin hut. The hut comprised of five shops. The plaintiffs possessed three shops. While defendant No. 12 possessed other two shops since 1994 and 1995 by way of purchase from defendant Nos. 1 to 6. 

 25. Further case of the plaintiffs is that in 1979, they found those three shops along with adjacent land, latrine and storeroom vacant and abandoned and entered. Since then they were doing business therein. They claim that they acquired title by adverse possession. 

 26. Defendant No. 12 opposed the claim of the plaintiffs saying that Abdul Motaleb, father of the plaintiffs, entered said shops as a tenant under the original owner, Hafez Mohammad Hossain. After his death, the plaintiffs continued as such. 

 31. Secondly, all the defence witnesses said that Abdul Motaleb, father of the plaintiffs, first possessed as tenant under original owner Hafez Mohammad Hossain. After his death, the plaintiffs continued as such. PW 1 just denied that. But such denial would not cut much ice. The defence case is more probable and believable. 

 32. Lastly, even if it is accepted that plaintiffs entered into the shops when they were vacant and abandoned, the possession of such shops would continue in law to be of the real owner unless and until the defendant acquires title by adverse possession. 

 35. In the circumstances, possession of the plaintiffs in the suit shops cannot be termed as adverse. Impugned judgment and decree of the trial Court declaring title of the plaintiff in the suit land therefore cannot be sustained in law. Appeal accordingly, succeeds.

parties:
Syed Rashid Ahmed ------ Petitioner
Versus
Idris Ullah and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Mr. Abdis Salam Mamun, J.: This Rule was issued calling upon the Opposite Parties to show cause as to why the impugned if their No.18 dated 11.4.1992 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Jagannathpur, in the Title Execution Case No.1 of 1991 should not be set aside. 

 2. Facts leading to the issuance of this Rule are that the Petitioner as Plaintiff instituted the Title Suit No.227 of 1962 in the Court of the Munsif, Sunamgonj on 14.12.1962 against the predecessors of the present Opposite Parties praying for .a decree for declaration of title in the suit land and for recovery for its khas possession. The suit was decreed on 30.5.1963 ex parte. 

 The Plaintiff-Petitioner thereafter filed the Title Execution Case No.26 of 1965 on 6.7.1965. 

 On 7.9.1965 a Miscellaneous Case, being No.42 of 1965 was filed by one Syed Enamul Hoq under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for setting aside the suit ex-parte decree on the ground that it was passed against him during his minority and in that Miscellaneous case, the Petitioner obtained an order staying all proceeding of the Title Execution 77.case No.26 of 1965. 

 In December, 1966, one Syeda Lutfunnessa and two others instituted the Title Suit No.255 of 1966 against the Petitioner and 17 others praying for a decree for declaration of their rights and title in the jote and that part of the suit land was covered by the decree of the Title Suit. No. 227 of 1962 also praying for confirmation of their possession with a further prayer for declaration of the ex-parte decree dated 30.5.1963 passed in the Title Suit No. 227 of 1962 is void, illegal and not binding upon the Plaintiffs and also for permanent injunction restraining of Defendants from evicting the Plaintiffs from the suit land. 

 By order dated 12.4.1967, passed in the Title Suit No. 225 of 1966, the decree-holder of the Title Suit No. 227 of 1962, i-e the Petitioner was restrained from taking over possession of the suit land by virtue of the decree passed in the Title Suit No. 227 of 1962 until further order. 

 Though in the Title Suit No. 225 of 1966, an order of injunction was passed restraining the Decree-Holder of the Title Suit No. 227 of 1962, from taking over possession until further order, but the executing Court passed an order in the Title Execution Case No. 26 of 1965 (Arising out of Title Suit No. 227 of 1962) On 6.6.1967 as follows: "The case is taken up today. As the Miscellaneous Case No.42 of 1965 had been disposed of in the month of November 1966, so the case is to be proceed with Requisites kept in the record. Decree-Holder to furnish Boat hire by 10.6.1967." And thereafter, the Execution Case was dismissed for default on 20.1.1968. According to the petitioner, the order for dismissal of the Execution case for default was an illegal order, passed without jurisdiction and is void ab initio. 

 On the other hand, the Title Suit No. 255 of 1966 was decreed on 29.3.1968 declaring that the Plaintiffs are co-sharers to the extent of 19/(5 )pies of share in the suit land and also declaring their joint possession. 

 The Petitioner then preferred an Appeal being the Title Appeal No.143 of 1968 against the said judgment and decree dated 29.3.1968 passed in the Title Suit No.255 of 1966. 

 On 21.3.1969 the Title Appeal No. 143 of 1968 was allowed in part by the judgment and decree passed by the Learned Appellate Court, modifying the decree passed by the trial court upon setting aside the decree for joint possession, holding that the appellant i-e. the present petitioner is in exclusive possession of the suit land and holding further that the Respondents-Plaintiffs will be at liberty to enter into possession to the extent of their share in the suit land through a suit for partition. 

 The Plaintiffs-Respondents have thereafter, preferred the Second Appeal No.614 of 1969 before the High Court at Dhaka against the said judgment and decree dated 21.3.1969 passed in the Title ...Appeal No. 143 of 1968 and during pendency of the said Second Appeal, further proceeding of the Title Execution Case No. 26 of 1965 was stayed at the instance of the appellants in the Civil Rule No. 920(S) of 1969. 

 On 23.3.1991 the petitioner filed the Title Execution Case No.1 of 1991 praying for the self-same relief, as it was prayed for, in the Title Execution Case No.26 of 1965. 

 On 1.12.1991 the judgment-debtor No. 1(Ka) filed an application in the Title Execution Case No.1 of 1991 under section 151 of the Code of Civil procedure praying for dismissal of the Execution Case on the ground of limitation. 

 On 27.1.1992 the judgment-debtor No. 2(Kha) filed another application under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for dismissal of the Execution Case on the ground of limitation. The decree-holder filed an objection to the application and by the impugned order, the Learned Munsif has been pleased to dismiss the Title Execution Case No.1 of 199 1 on the ground of limitation. 

 3. The Decree-Holder has thereafter preferred this application under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the instant Rule on 19.7.1992 on the grounds that the order dated 20,1.1968 passed in the Title Execution Case No. 26 of 1965 is neither final order nor it was sustainable in law. The Learned Munsif has committed an error in law by not treating the subsequent application for execution, in substance, to be one for revival or continuation of the original application of the Title Execution Case No.26 of 1965 and thus, there was no question of limitation. The Learned Munsif has also erred in law in not computing the period of limitation from 4.6.1990, the date on which, the Civil Petition for Special Leave of Appeal No: 211 of 1987 was dismissed. 

 4. Dr. Naim Ahmed, the Learned Advocate, appearing for the Petitioner, after placing the impugned order submits that the Title Execution Case No.26 of 1965 was purported to be dismissed on 20.1.1968 on a date on which an order of injunction was in force over it issued in the Title Suit No.255 of 1966 also restraining the decree-holder from taking over possession of the suit land and as such the said order of dismissal is illegal., inoperative and void ab initio and cannot be treated as a judicial order and consequently, the Title Execution Case Noll of 1991 is merely a petition for revival or continuation of the original execution petition and not for starting an Execution Case afresh. 

 Relying upon the cases of Government of Rajsthan and another Vs. Sangram Singh and others, reported in AIR 1962 Raj (FB) 43, Chhatter Singh Vs. Kamal Singh, reported in. AIR 1927 All (FB) 16 and Shah Newaz Ebne Mostaque and others Vs. Shah Alam and others, reported in 55 DLR (AD) 69, the learned Advocate submits that an Execution application must be deemed to be pending so long as no final order disposing of it judicially has been passed thereupon. A subsequent application in such a case for execution will be deemed to be one merely for the continuation or revival of the original proceeding and where the circumstances are such that the decree-holder can ask for a revival of an earlier proceeding, even an application, which is in form one for execution, will be considered to be one for revival or continuation of earlier proceeding and that the decree holder is not required to file an application for proceeding with the pending execution case as it is the duty of the Court to proceed with the same suo motu. Such a pending execution case is not hit by limitation. 

 The Learned Advocate further submits that the Learned Munsif in dismissing Execution case has erred in law in holding that the order passed in the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal is not a decree, in .view of the provisions of the Article 182(2) of the Limitation Act, which according to the Learned Advocate, also includes a 'final order'. The Order dated 4.6.1990 is a judgment passed on merit in which the Appellate Division has observed that 'the subsequent Title Suit No.255 of 1966 was filed to •deprive the Plaintiff of the Title Suit No.227 of 1962 and with a view to reap the benefit of the decree obtained against the trespasser', and as such, the Learned Advocate contends, it was a final order within the meaning of Article 182(2) of the Limitation Act. 

 10. In the instant Case, the litigation started between the parties on 14.12.1962 upon institution of the Title Suit No.227 of 1962 in the 'Court of the Munsif Sunamganj and its exparte decree on 30.5.1963 and reached to its finality on 4.6.1990 upon dismissal of Civil Petition fro Special Leave to Appeal No.211 of 1987. 

 The order of dismissal passed in the Execution Case No.26 of 1966, was admittedly passed at a time when there was an order of stay in force on the execution proceeding and as such, the order of dismissal was passed in utter violation of law and efface illegal and the Opposite Party is not entitled to reap any benefit out of the said illegal order. 

 The impugned Order No.18 dated 11.4.1992 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Jagannathpur, in the Title Execution Case No.1 of 1.991 is hereby set aside and the Execution Case No.26 of 1966 is restored to its file and number on the basis of the application filed, upon which the Execution case No.1 of 1991 was started. 

 The learned Assistant Judge, Jagannathpur is directed to proceed with the Title Execution Case No.26 of 1966 from the stage where it was pending before the order of stay was passed.

parties:
Sukkada Bala Gope ----- Appellant.
Vs.
Pran Hari Gope being died his heris ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
"Learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that original R.S. Khatian No. 2324 being in the name of the original owner Kamini, Probodh and six others and suit dag No. 7066 having been recorded in the name of kamini and Probodh Chandra Ghose, father of the petitioner Sukada Bala Gope having purchased. 08 decimals from Kamini Bala vide deed No. 1175 dated 2.5.1932 Ext. A and Kamini Bala having been admitted as the owner of plot by both the parties and Prododh having purchased the suit plot from Kamini Bala, the recorded owner, vide Exhibit-A and the said deed being earlier than the deed of the plaintiff-respondent's predecessor and the said deed Ext. A having not been challenged in any court of law High Court Division acted illegally in making the rule absolute. 

 3. The facts relevant for disposal of the appeal are that the respondents as the plaintiff filed Other Suit No. 141 of 1984 in the court of the Munsif, Sitakunda against the petitioner for declaration of title to the suit land alleging that the suit land originally belonged to Kamini Bala Ghosh who sold the same to Ramoni Mohan sold the same to Joshada Sundari Saha by a registered kabala dated 5.2.1944 who died leaving Sudamoni Saha as her son's widow and the said Sudamoni Saha sold the suit land to the plaintiff by a kabala dated 9.1.1978 and since then he is in possession of the same. Defendant's name having been wrongly recorded in the B.S. khatian plaintiff filed the suit for declaration of title. 

 4. Defendant-appellant contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations and asserting that original owner Kamani Bala sold entire suit land to Probodh Chandra by a registered kabala dated 2.5.1932 and since then Probodh owned and possessed the same and leased out half portion of the suit land to the appellant by a registered patta dated 19.11.1940 and subsequently died leaving behind the appellant as his only heir and as such defendant-appellant's name was correctly recorded in the B.S. khatian and he has the right, title and possession of the same and the plaintiff has no title and possession and filed the suit to harass the defendant-appellant. 

 6. Mr. Mohammad Ozair Farooq, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellants submits that the original R.S. Khatian being No. 2324 standing in the name of Kamini, Probadh and 6 others in respect of the suit plot No. 7066 and Kamini has disposed of the entire. 08 decimals of plot No. 7066 by kabala dated 2.5.1932 in favour of Probadh Chandra Ghose who in his turn leased out half of the land in favour of the appellant vide registered patta dated 19.11.1940 and the rest having been inherited by the appellant and the entire Khatian was recorded in the name of the appellant, the High Court Division erred in law in not holding that the suit for declaration of title is not maintainable and that Ext. A registered kabala dated 2.5.1932 is earlier in point of time as against the kabala of the plaintiff dated 11.7.1935 from the admitted owner Kamini Bala Ghosh thereby the appellant has acquired title on the basis of Patta dated 19.11.1940 Ext. B and inheritance and that the possession of the appellant is further evident from Ext. C series rent receipts, the High Court Division misread and misconceived the documents and the evidence of D.Ws. Both as regards title and possession and according erred in law in not dismissing the suit. 

 7. Mr. Subrata Chowdhury, the learned Counsel appearing for the respondent submitted that from the pleading and the evidence on record, both oral and documentary it is evident that the predecessor-in-interest Soudhamoni has been possessing the suit land inasmuch as B.S. Plot No. 7066 is different from R.S. Plot. The plaintiff has based her title on registered kabala dated 9.1.1978 and that original owner Kamini Bala has transferred the suit land to Ramoni Mohan Das by registered kabala dated 11.5.1935 (Ext. 5) who in his tern transferred to Joshada Sundari Saha by registered kabala dated 5.4.1944 (Ext. 4) and Joshada's only heir Saudhamoni sold the same to the plaintiff on 9.1.1978 (Ext. 3) 

 8. It appears that the High Court Division on consideration of the material evidence on record arrived at the findings that the document filed by the plaintiff in support of their title and possession correctly and clearly proved the title and possession in the suit land and the documents filed by the defendants were not relating to the suit land. The defendant though claimed title and possession partly by registered patta but did not file the kabuliyat and rent receipt showing that the patta was acted upon, mores, the patta do not relate to the suit land so is the case with Kabala dated 2.5.1932. On the contrary, by way of successive transfers relating back to the admitted original owner Kamini, the suit land devolved upon the plaintiff by purchase vide kabala dated 9.1.1978 (Ext. 3); the plaintiff as well proved rent receipts and led oral evidence showing their possession in the suit land. The trial Court as well found the title and possession of the suit land but the Court of appeal below without adverting to the reasoning of the trial Court set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court even without reversing the finding therein.

parties:
Md. Abu Daud Sarder ----- Appellant
Vs.
The State and another ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
6. The appellant then moved the High Court Division seeking quashing of the proceeding of the C.R. case stating inter-alia that prior to the filing of the petition of complaint he on 3rd April, 1993 (petition of complaint was filed on 20, September, 1993 and the learned Magistrate examined complainant under section 200 Cr. PC. on 21 September, 1993) filed Title Suit No. 62 of 1993 in the Court of Assistant Judge, satkhira impleading the complainant and others as defendants seeking declaration of title and confirmation of possession as regard the land of deed No. 86 of 8-1-1976 and that in the said Title Suit he has filed the original deed No. 86 dated January 8, 1976 along with the plaint and that summons of the said Title Suit has duly been served upon the respondent No. 2 and others but instead of entering appearance in the Title Suit the respondent No. 2 has filed the Criminal Case i.e. C.R. Case No. 174 of 1993. 

 7. It was the contention of the appellant before the High Court Division that since the original deed No. 86 of January 8, 1976 has been filed prior to the filing of petition of complaint and issuance of summons in connection with C.R. Case No. 174 of 1993 before the Court of Assistant Judge in Title Suit No. 62 of 1993 and that the said document having been sent for obtaining opinion of the Hand Writing Expert and the report of the Hand Writing Expert as awaiting and that adjudication of issue as to genuineness of the deed in question as is pending before the Court of Assistant Judge, the proceeding of the C.R. Case being an abuse of the process of the Court and that also harassing as such the same is liable to be quashed. 

 10. The undisputed fact is that Title Suit No. 62 of 1993 relating to the land of the deed No. 86 dated January 8, 1976 has been filed on April 3, 1993 and that the C.R. Case No. 174 of 1993 has been initiated upon the petition of complaint filed on September 20, 1993 and that complainant was examined on September, 21, 1993 and cognizance was taken on December, 11, 1993. 

 13. The deed dated January 8, 1976 has been filed by the appellant before the Court of Assistant Judge in support of his claim as regard the property in respect where he has sought for declaration of title and confirmation of possession. The said document has been sent to the Hand Writing Expert or opinion and the report of the Hand Writing Expert yet to be received by the said Court and as such the genuineness or otherwise of the said deed in the background of pendency of the Title Suit awaits adjudication. The question that calls for determination is whether the deed No. 86 dated 8-1-1976 which along with the plaint of Title Suit the appellant has already filed in the Court of Assistant Judge, is a forged document as defined in section 463 of the Penal Code and that appellant has given in evidence such document being a forged one and if it is in the affirmative then whether the instant criminal proceeding is barred at the instance of Respondent No. 2 in view of Provision of Section 195(1)(c) Cr. PC. As seen from the materials on record the questioned deed has been sent by the Court of Assistant Judge to the Hand Writing Expert for examination and report. This shows that the deed in question has been used by the appellant in the Title Suit and would be relied upon by the appellant as piece of evidence in support the claim being the subject matter of the Title Suit No. 62 of 1993. In the light of the provision of section 195(1)(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure if upon conclusion of trial of the Title Suit the court finds the deed in question not genuine or in other words forged, then as the deed has been used by the appellant in the court as genuine in-spite of the same being forged it is for the court to make decision whether to proceed against the appellant for the offence said to have been committed under the provision in section 195(1)(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure or not. Since before the initiation of the Criminal case i.e. C.r. Case No. 174 of 1993 the deed has been produced and used before the Civil Court in support the relief prayed for in the suit and that the suit in which said deed has been used is still pending and consequently the genuineness or otherwise of the deed relating to which criminal proceeding has been started at the instance of the Respondent No. 2, who is a party in the suit as defendant, awaits adjudication, as such because of the provision of clause (c) of Sub-section (1) of section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure the respondent No. 2 at his level is barred from initiating criminal proceeding on the allegation that the deed dated January 8, 1976 is a forged one. Even if on the termination of trial of the Title Suit the document in question is found by the court otherwise than being genuine then also Respondent No. 2 under the law would not be competent to initiate criminal proceeding on the allegation deed in question is forged as has been given in evidence in the trial. In view of the provision of clause (c) of section 195(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Respondent No. 2 may approach the court for taking appropriate step against the appellant since he used a deed in the suit as genuine inspite of knowing the same being forged and then it is for the court alone that may decide as to whether it would initiate proceeding against the appellant for committing one of the offence or more as mentioned in clause (c) of section 195 (1) Cr. PC. 

 15. The judgment and order of the High Court Division of 14th June 1998 in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 160 of 1995 is set aside and the proceeding of C.R. Case No. 174 of 1993 (Sadar) T.R. Case No. 95 of 1994 of the Court of Magistrate 1st Class, Satkhira, is quashed. However on termination of trial of the Title Suit No. 62 of 1993 of the Court of Assistant Judge, Satkhira, if deed No. 86 dated 8-1-1976 is held to be otherwise than genuine, in that case court would be quite competent to take steps as per law to start criminal proceeding against the appellant.
