parties:
Abu Daud (Md) Sarder ------ Appellant
Vs.
State and another ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
6. The appellant then moved the High Court Division seeking quashing of the proceeding of the C.R. case stating, inter alia, that prior to the filing of the petition of complaint he on 3rd April, 1993 (petition of complaint was filed on 20th September, 1993 and the learned Magistrate examined complainant under section 200 Cr.P.C on 21 September, 1993) filed Title Suit No. 62 of 1993 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Satkhira impleading the complainant and others as defendants seeking declaration of title and confirmation of possession as regard the land of Deed No. 86 of 8-1-1976 and that in the said Title Suit he has filed the original Deed No. 86 dated January 8, 1976 along with the plaint and that summons of the said Title Suit has duly been served upon the respondent No. 2 and others but instead of entering appearance in the Title Suit the respondent No. 2 has filed the Criminal Case i.e. C.R. Case No. 174 of 1993. 

 7. It was the contention of the appellant before the High Court Division that since the original Deed No. 86 of January 8, 1976 has been filed prior to the filing of petition of complaint and issuance of summons in connection with C.R. Case No. 174 of 1993 before the Court of Assistant Judge in Title Suit No. 62 of 1993 and that the said document having been sent for obtaining opinion of the Hand Writing Expert and the report of the Hand Writing Expert was awaiting and that adjudication of issue as to genuineness of the deed in question as is pending before the Court of Assistant Judge, the proceeding of the C.R. Case being an abuse of the process of the Court and that also harassing, as such, the same is liable to be quashed. 

 10. The undisputed fact is that Title Suit No. 62 of 1993 relating to the land of the deed No. 86 dated January 8, 1976 has melt April 3, 1993 and that the C.R. Case No. 174 of 1993 has been initiated upon the petition of complaint filed on September 20, 1993 and that complainant was examined on September 21, 1993 and cognizance was taken on December 11, 1993. 

 13. The deed dated January 8, 1976 has been filed by the appellant before the Court of Assistant Judge in support of his claim as regard the property in respect where he has sought for declaration of title and confirmation of possession. The said document has been sent to the Hand Writing Expert for opinion and the report of the Hand Writing Expert is yet to be received by the said Court and, as such, the genuineness or otherwise of the said Deed in the background of pendency of the Title Suit awaits adjudication. The question that calls for determination is, whether the deed No. 86 dated 8-1-1976 which along with the plaint of Title Suit the appellant has already filed in the Court of Assistant Judge, is a forged document as defined in section 463 of the Penal Code and that appellant has given in evidence such document being a forged one and if it is in the affirmative then whether the instant criminal proceeding is barred at the instance of respondent No. 2 in view of provision of section 195(1)(c) Cr.P.C. As seen from the materials on record the questioned deed has been sent by the Court of Assistant Judge to the Hand Writing Expert for examination and report. This shows that the deed in question has been used by the appellant in the Title Suit and would be relied upon by the appellant as piece of evidence in support of the claim being the subject matter of the Title Suit No. 62 of 1993. In the light of the provision of section 195(1)(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure if upon conclusion of trial of the Title Suit the court finds the deed in question not genuine or, in other words, forged, then as the deed has been used by the appellant in the court as genuine in spite of the same being forged it is for the court to make decision whether to proceed against the appellant for the offence said to have been committed under the provision of section 195(1)(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure or not. Since before the initiation of the criminal case i.e. C.R. Case No. 174 of 1993, the deed has been produced and used before the civil Court in support of the relief prayed for in the suit and that the suit in which said deed has been used is still pending and consequently, the genuineness or otherwise of the deed relating to which criminal proceeding has been started at the instance of the respondent No. 2, who is a party in the suit as defendant, awaits adjudication, as such, because of the provision of clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure the respondent No. 2 at his level is barred from initiating criminal proceeding on the allegation that the deed dated January 8, 1976 is a forged one. Even if on the termination of trial of the Title Suit the document in question is found by the court otherwise than being genuine then also respondent No. 2 under the law would not be competent to initiate criminal proceeding on the allegation that deed in question is forged as has been given in evidence in the trial. In view of the provision of clause (c) of section 195(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure respondent No. 2 may approach the court for taking appropriate step against the appellant since he used a deed in the suit as genuine in spite of knowing the same as being forged and then it is for the court alone that may decide as to whether it would initiate proceeding against the appellant for committing one of the offences or more as mentioned in clause (c) of section 195(1) Cr.P.C. 

 The judgment and order of the High Court Division of 14th June, 1998 in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 160 of 1995 is set aside and the proceeding of C.R Case No. 174 of 1993. (Sadar)/TR Case No. 95d of 1994 of the Court of Magistrate 1st Class, Satkhira, is quashed. However, on termination of trial of the Title Suit No. 62 of 1993 of the Court of Assistant Judge, Satkhira, if deed No. 86 dated 8-1-1976 is held to be otherwise than genuine, in that case court would be quite competent to take steps as per law to start criminal proceeding against the appellant.

Ali Azam ----- Petitioner 
Vs.
Md Majibullah ----- Opposite Party
full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the Judgment and decree dated 19-7-1998 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Noakhali in Title Appeal No. 15 of 1998 reversing the Judgment and decree dated 14-1-1998 passed by Senior Assistant Judge in-Charge, Second Court, Sadar Noakhali, in Title Suit No. 69 of 1991. 

 2. The relevant facts for the disposal of this Rule, in short, are that the petitioner Ali Azam as plaintiff instituted the instant suit for declaration that the defendant is his benamder in respect of the land as described in the schedule of the plaint. They are full brothers. The plaintiff joined in service in 1956. On the other hand, the defendant joined in 1972. Their father served in a Sub-Registrar's office. He had two wives, two sons and two daughters by his first wife and one son and two daughters by his second wife. He was a resident of village Mokimpar. After erosion of property in the river, their father took shelter in the house of his elder brother at village Shyampur in 1950. He had no property. The plaintiff gave in marriage of his sisters and bore all the educational expenditures of younger brother from his earnings. The plaintiff's father retired, from his service in 1968. The plaintiff purchased 2.50 acre of land as described in the schedule 'Ka' of the plaint from one Yunus Mia by a kabala deed dated 4-4-1962 at consideration of Taka 1,000. He also purchased 1.25 acre of land from Momtaz and others by another kabala deed dated 6-4-1964 at consideration of Taka 500. He again purchased 2.86-1/2 acres of land from one Amar Krishna Routh and others by a kabala deed dated 10-11-1969 at consideration of Taka 1500. He also purchased 1.64 acre of land from one Amyo Prova Routh by another kabala deed dated 12-1-1970 at a consideration of Taka 500. He himself purchased the stamp papers of those kabala deeds and paid considerations. The defendant did not pay any consideration and registration cost for those four kabala deeds. At the time of purchase of those lands, the defendant was unemployed. He was a simple name lender of the plaintiff. The plaintiff mutated his name in the khatian and has been paying rent to the Government. Recently, the defendant claimed title in the suit land and, as such, the plaintiff filed the instant suit. 

 6. Mr Sarder Abul Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that it is evident that the plaintiff was a government servant. As there was a bar to purchase more land in his own name the plaintiff purchased the suit land in the benami of his brother the defendant. He paid entire consideration from his own fund. The title documents of the suit land were produced before the court by the plaintiff. The plaintiff has exclusively possessed the entire suit land. In such view of the matter the learned appellate Court, without proper consideration and appreciation of the evidence on record, erroneously dismissed the suit reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court. 

 7. Mr Abul Kalam Chowdhury, the learned. Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party, submits that the instant transactions were not benami transactions and the suit in its present form was not maintainable. He further submits that some of the witnesses of plaintiff, particularly PW 9 in his evidence, admitted that both the parties have been possessing the suit land. He further submits that although the title documents of the land had been produced by the plaintiff but the same is not unnatural because the plaintiff is the full brother of the defendant. As the defendant has been serving as an officer of Trading Corporation of Bangladesh, so naturally, the title documents are to be kept in the custody of his full brother who has been living in his paternal house. It is evident that at the time of recent survey operation, the plaintiff brought the title documents from, he defendant in order to record their name in the khatian. He further submits that the plaintiff failed to prove motive of purchase of the suit land in the benami of the defendant. He further submits that the plaintiff and the defendant are full brothers and they purchased the suit land from the money given by their mother, father and from their own funds. That is, the lements of banani transaction are not present in the instant case. In such view of the matter, the learned appellate Court rightly dismissed the suit reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court. 

 "It is well settled that the burden of proving that a particular sale is benami and the apparent purchaser is not the real owner, always rests on the person asserting it to be so. This burden has to be strictly discharged by adducing legal evidence, a definite character which. would either directly prove the fact of benami or establish circumstances unerringly and reasonably raising an inference of that fact. The essence of a benami is the intention of the party or parties concerned; and not when such intention is shrouded in a thick veil which cannot be easily pierced through. But such difficulties do not relieve the person asserting the transaction to be benami of any part of the serious onus that rests on him; nor justify the acceptance of mere conjectures or surmises, as a substitute for proof. The reason is that a deed is a solemn document prepared and executed after considerable deliberation, and the person expressly shown as the purchaser of transaction in the deed starts with the initial presumption in his favour that the apparent state of affairs is the real state of affairs. Though the question, whether a particular sale is benami or not is largely one of fact; and for determining this question, no absolute formulae or acid test, uniformly applicable in all situations, can be laid down, yet in weighing the probabilities and for gathering the relevant indicia, the courts are usually guided by these circumstances, (1) the source from which the purchase money came; (2) the nature and possession of the property, after the purchase; (3) motive, if any for giving the transaction a benami colour, (4) the position of the parties and the relationship, if any, between the claimant and the alleged benamder, (5) the custody of the title deeds after the sale and (6) the conduct of the parties concerned in dealing with the property after the sale. 

 3.	Possession of the title deeds. 

 14. It is true that the plaintiff produced the original documents relating to title of the suit land. We have already found that the original documents were executed and registered in the name of two brothers namely, the plaintiff and the defendant. So, it is not natural that those documents are to be kept either in the custody of the plaintiff or in the custody of defendant. So, in the instant case I think that the custody of the document is not very much material. Although the plaintiff has paid rent to the government as it appears from the Exhibit 3 series but it also appears from those rent receipts that the plaintiff paid rent just before the institution of the instant suit perhaps, the same was done only to take preparation to file the instant suit.
